method: Per-PR collaboration-pattern comparison in agent era: Markov-chain/EM clustering of reviewer-type sequences into 10 patterns; Scott-Knott ESD for efficiency rank; chi-square with Bonferroni for smells

quality_notes: Time almost exclusively positive; exceptions are PR time-to-merge and time-to-review/approval (mixed: one significant increase, one significant decrease, one null); AI assessment 5/8 negative (62%)

method: Extraction of confounders explicitly discussed in relation to productivity effects (stage 1 only)
population: 27 stage-1 papers
metric: Confounder coverage
effect_size: 44 unique confounders in 15 of 27 papers; median 1 per paper; 21 of the 44 from one paper (Becker et al., METR); top: developer experience 6 papers, AI tool experience 4, project/task complexity 4, project involvement 2, usage approach 2, usage frequency 2; 38 confounders reported once; juniors benefit more in 5 papers, seniors mixed (smaller gains in 2, no significant effect in 1, exclusive benefit in 1, decline in 1); greater task complexity linked to less positive impact in 3 papers
seniority_split: juniors tend to gain more; senior evidence mixed (paper counts as listed)
codebase_context: task complexity discussed in 4 papers; codebase maturity and verification cost are not among the review's named recurring confounders
independence_flags: Publicly funded; no vendor tie
quality_notes: Only confounders explicitly discussed are captured, so absence from the list reflects reporting practice as well as the field; review itself says no generalisable conclusions can be drawn on confounder effects

era: E1/E2 (no E3 study identified in the corpus)
method: Corpus inspection (search terms, reference list, text)
population: 45 papers from 2023 onward
metric: Agentic-era coverage
effect_size: No occurrence of agent, agentic, Claude Code, Cursor or Devin in the text; search templates use chatgpt, LLM, coding assistant, chatbot, copilot; tools studied are Copilot, ChatGPT and similar; one included paper (Becker et al. 2025, early-2025 tools) is the nearest to agentic use and is not labelled as such by the review; review does not state a scarcity of agentic evidence
independence_flags: Publicly funded; no vendor tie
quality_notes: Reviewer inference from text and reference list, not a statement in the paper; manuscript received 2026-03-26, accepted 2026-06-18; stage 1 includes the METR paper as the only study with a clear negative primary finding

method: Authors' implications for researchers and practitioners
population: Review conclusions
metric: Measurement recommendations
effect_size: Report explicitly whether results are perceived productivity, observed behavioural change or statistically tested effects and do not treat them as interchangeable; define the productivity dimensions assessed; include human-centred outcomes (satisfaction, well-being) alongside speed and output; treat context (experience, tool experience, task complexity) as part of study design; do not conflate productivity gains with tool quality, since AI assessment trends negative while productivity trends positive; avoid Likert items that cannot express a negative effect
independence_flags: Publicly funded; no vendor tie
quality_notes: Recommendations are for research design; applicability to internal instrumentation is by extension. DevEx guidance cited: combine subjective perceptions with objective process indicators

era: E3 (tool ranking; list mixes E1-E3 products)
method: Opt-in web survey, self-reported
population: Developers answering SO survey, n=12,255 on coding-agent question (30,903 valid overall); self-selected, no weighting
metric: Coding agent/assistant used in past year (multi-select ranking)
effect_size: Claude Code 65.5% (8,030), GitHub Copilot 58.7% (7,196), OpenAI Codex 29.5%, Cursor 25.5%, Google Antigravity 16.0%, Devin 2.9%; n=12,255
direction: Claude Code leads; popularity ranking only
independence_flags: Stack Overflow commercial AI interests; self-selected respondents; list mixes autocomplete and agentic products, mode of use not specified
quality_notes: Not a measure of agentic adoption share; base is those answering the question; tool popularity not value

era: E2/E3 mixed (coding assistants and agents bundled)
method: Opt-in web survey, self-reported
population: Developers, n=17,464 (AISelect); n=14,478 (AIFreq)
metric: Adoption and frequency of AI at work (AISelect, AIFreq)
effect_size: Use AI coding assistants or agents 65.9% (11,509 of 17,464); AI agents or automated workflows 26.2% (4,582); no AI tools 17.2%; of coding assistant users 73.0% use daily (n=14,478 for AIFreq)
direction: High adoption; agents/automated workflows used by about a quarter
independence_flags: SO commercial interest; self-selection toward engaged developers
quality_notes: Daily share is of tool users; blog wording 'of AI users' is inaccurate; no trend comparison in tables

method: Opt-in web survey, self-reported
population: Daily AI users, n=10,926 (AIDaily); 'How much of your workday do you use AI tools to help you work?'
metric: Self-estimated hours of AI use per workday among daily users
effect_size: 4+ hours 30.9%; 2-4 hours 24.1%; 1-2 hours 25.3%; under 1 hour 19.2% combined; 2+ hours 55.0% (n=10,926)
independence_flags: SO commercial interest; self-selection
quality_notes: Hub's '80% at least an hour a day' is of daily users, not all respondents; time use is not value

method: Opt-in web survey, self-reported
population: Developers, n=14,304 (AITrust); 'How much do you trust the output from AI tools or AI agents as part of your workflow?'
metric: Trust in AI output
effect_size: Trust when easily verified 48.0% (6,872); many tasks not important decisions 16.3%; low-risk only 16.3%; do not trust for most tasks 12.3%; many tasks including important decisions 6.6% (949 of 14,304)
direction: Trust is conditional on verifiability; very few extend it to important decisions
seniority_split: Early-career 4% trust for important decisions vs 6.6% overall (band and base not stated)
independence_flags: SO commercial interest; self-selection; wording differs from 2025 trust-accuracy item (33%) so no trend

method: Opt-in web survey, self-reported
population: Developers, n=14,428 (AISentiment); experience splits base not stated
metric: Attitude toward using AI tools or agents at work
effect_size: 62% favourable (31.6% very, 30.4% somewhat); 21.5% unfavourable; favourable 53% at 1-5 years vs 69% at 16+ years; 71% among daily users (blog); n=14,428
direction: Majority favourable; more senior more favourable
independence_flags: SO commercial interest; self-selection
quality_notes: Sentiment is not impact evidence; experience-split bases unstated; 2025 reported 60% favourable on differently worded item

method: Opt-in web survey, self-reported
population: Developers, n=14,341 (AIComplex); 'How well do the AI tools or agents you use handle complex tasks?'
metric: Self-rated AI performance on complex tasks
effect_size: Very well 16.0%; good but not great 38.8%; neither 14.4%; bad 16.0%; very poor 8.0%; don't use/don't know 6.9% (n=14,341); 45% of infrequent users rate bad or very poor
direction: Few rate it very well; a quarter rate it bad or very poor
independence_flags: SO commercial interest; self-selection
quality_notes: 'Complex' undefined; brownfield not distinguished; no daily-user figure given

method: Opt-in web survey, self-reported
population: Developers, n=13,162 (AIWorkNext); multi-select 'What do you usually do before using an AI-generated answer for a development task?'
metric: Stated verification practices before using AI output
effect_size: Run locally 76.5%; compare against codebase context 63.9%; inspect tests/security 53.0%; read docs 38.0%; use as-is 9.6%; ask coworker 6.9% (n=13,162)
direction: Verification is the stated norm; about 90% do not use as-is
codebase_context: Codebase-context comparison implies brownfield checking but not measured
independence_flags: SO commercial interest; stated habits not observed behaviour; likely socially desirable answers
quality_notes: No item on time spent verifying or on 'almost right' output found

method: Opt-in web survey, self-reported
population: Developers, n=12,734 (AIImpact usefulness) and n=12,547 (AIWork current use)
metric: Perceived usefulness of AI by SDLC stage
effect_size: Useful or very useful: implementation 74.6% (T3/T4), debugging/refactoring 72.6% (T8/T5), documentation 65.7% (T10), review 64.5% (T7), architecture exploration 59.1% (T2), design 49.2%, communication 35.0% (n=12,734); current use: tests 58.1% (T6), tickets/requirements 27.8% (T1) (n=12,547)
direction: Useful for code-centric stages, weaker for design and communication
independence_flags: SO commercial interest; perception only; implementation not split T3/T4
quality_notes: Computed combined figures; press release's debugging 66% is the satisfaction figure

method: Opt-in web survey, self-reported
population: Developers, n=12,125 (AISat); satisfaction change by task
metric: Self-reported change in satisfaction with task since using AI
effect_size: Improved/decreased/no change: debugging-refactoring 66.1/10.5/23.4; documentation 60.6/9.8/29.6; implementation 60.1/19.9/19.9; review 55.3/11.9/32.8; communication 32.7/17.9/49.5 (n=12,125)
direction: Improved for most; implementation most polarised (19.9% decreased)
independence_flags: SO commercial interest; computed from table categories; wording not captured verbatim
quality_notes: Satisfaction not productivity; no measured counterpart

method: Opt-in web survey, self-reported
population: Developers, n=12,547 (AIWork)
metric: Current AI use for deploying, operating and troubleshooting production
effect_size: Use now 19.9%; expect more 23.3%; do not use and don't plan to 36.0%; not part of workflow 22.0% (n=12,547); compare generating code in familiar area 69.3% use now, 9.0% won't use
direction: AI is largely kept out of production operations; technology page says adoption falls as complexity and operational risk rise
independence_flags: SO commercial interest; self-selection; stated intentions
quality_notes: Cross-tab behind the 'adoption drops with complexity' statement not captured

method: Opt-in web survey, self-reported (organisational policy)
population: Developers, n=13,167 (AIUse), n=13,144 (AIToolSwitch); blog cost items base not stated
metric: Organisational AI governance, cost controls, usage limits
effect_size: Use optional 29.7%; approved tools and guidance 24.0%; measured in performance 10.2% (n=13,167); switched tool because previous became too expensive, limited or unavailable 3.3%, lower cost 6.4% (n=13,144); blog only: usage limits 38%, spend review 28%, limiting who can use AI 25%, 21% say org spending more (base and wording not captured)
direction: Governance mostly light; cost controls emerging but thinly evidenced
independence_flags: SO commercial interest; respondent-reported org practice; blog cost items untraceable to tables
quality_notes: Cost-governance numbers are blog-only and unverified; no token or licence spend; RQ4 stays thin

method: Opt-in web survey, self-reported
population: Developers, n=13,857 (AIAvoid)
metric: Reasons for avoiding AI at work or school (skill formation)
effect_size: Do not avoid 41.3%; losing job skills or training a replacement 17.1% (2,367); moral/ethical 15.2%; privacy/security 13.0%; environmental 8.2%; lack of training 2.6% (n=13,857); 58.7% cite some reason
direction: Skills loss is the top-cited reason for avoidance, ahead of ethics and security
independence_flags: SO commercial interest; avoidance reasons are attitudes, not evidence of skill erosion
quality_notes: Combines skills loss with replacement fear in one option, so cognitive-debt signal is diluted

method: Online between-subjects randomised user study; Aider agent (GPT-4.1) vs no-code-access chatbot (GPT-4.1); 50 min task
population: n=54 CS students (17 BSc/31 MSc/11 PhD recruited n=59, 5 dropped) at two US colleges; 27 per arm; mean 5.4 yrs coding, 16.2 months AI use; no professionals
metric: Initial-task code accuracy (proportion of 15 rubric rules met, Gemini-3.1 Pro judge) and time-to-submission (secondary)
effect_size: Agent users more accurate and quicker than chatbot users; exact means/SEs/test statistics NOT in text (Figure 4 only); n=27 per arm; no CI or p reported in text for this outcome
direction: agent faster and more accurate than constrained chatbot
cost_data: none reported (prompts per user in initial task: agent 5.8+/-0.4 vs chatbot 11.6+/-2.5)
seniority_split: not split (BG-ability regression only: BG predicts initial accuracy in chatbot users but not agent users)
codebase_context: greenfield 'zic-zac-zoe' 5x5 game in HTML/CSS/JS, three files, single task
independence_flags: none (NSF-funded academic; no vendor)
quality_notes: comparator is a chatbot that may only emit <=5-line generic snippets, so it approximates hand-writing not typical chat use; magnitude unrecoverable from text; in-progress preprint v1

method: Randomised between-subjects; 12 LLM-tailored multiple-choice comprehension questions about the user's own code (6 recall, 6 reasoning), answered without seeing the code
population: n=54 CS students (17 BSc/31 MSc/11 PhD recruited n=59, 5 dropped) at two US colleges; 27 per arm; mean 5.4 yrs coding, 16.2 months AI use; no professionals
metric: Code comprehension accuracy (proportion correct); skill-formation theme
effect_size: Agent users substantially lower; Figure 1 caption: p<0.002, Cohen's d>0.80 (test unnamed; group means not in text); persists after adding initial accuracy (agent coefficient still significantly lower); n=27 per arm; reduction holds for 3 of 4 question types (not 'change' questions)
seniority_split: not split; BG ability strongly predicts comprehension in both arms (adj R2 0.40 -> 0.42 when initial accuracy added)
codebase_context: greenfield single website task, same-session recall
independence_flags: none
quality_notes: questions generated by GPT-5.2 and validated (98-100% pass rates, distractor guess check 0.38 vs 0.5 chance); exploratory per authors; no multiple-comparison correction mentioned

method: Randomised between-subjects; 20 min extension of own code using chatbot only (agent arm given 5 min chatbot warm-up); 12-rule rubric, LLM-judged
population: n=54 CS students (17 BSc/31 MSc/11 PhD recruited n=59, 5 dropped) at two US colleges; 27 per arm; mean 5.4 yrs coding, 16.2 months AI use; no professionals
metric: Extension-task accuracy without agent
effect_size: Agent users 'not much higher' than chatbot users: no clear difference (exact means not in text); simplified path model: opposing indirect effects (agent -> higher initial accuracy -> higher extension; agent -> lower comprehension -> lower extension) offset, total effect and direct effect non-significant; per Figure 1 caption agent edge reverses when controlling for initial accuracy; adj R2 for extension 0.05 -> 0.22 (Fig 7 caption) or 0.34 (Sec 4.3 text) when initial accuracy and comprehension added
direction: null on total effect; comprehension deficit not shown to cost extension performance overall
seniority_split: not split; BG ability weakly predicts extension accuracy (adj R2=0.05), in chatbot but not agent users
codebase_context: extension of own greenfield code in same session (about 70 min after start)
independence_flags: none
quality_notes: NULL total effect, reported as such; mediation is observational within a randomised design; paper's two R2 values for same model are inconsistent (0.34 vs 0.22); 20 min is a short horizon

method: Observational sub-analysis within agent arm (n=27); LLM-labelled prompt strategies (152 prompts; 90% author agreement, 94% Gemini-author)
population: 27 agent-arm students (subset of the n=54 study); strategies unbalanced (n=25 users used copying at least once)
metric: Mean comprehension by prompting strategy; regression with BG control
effect_size: Mean comprehension: explain codebase 0.635 (n=6), copy criteria 0.654 (n=25), iterative debugging 0.692 (n=5), criteria turned into syntax 0.743 (n=9); users can appear in several groups; regression (BG-controlled): copy -0.4685, exploratory -0.7447, debugging -0.3378 relative to technical prompts, no CIs or p reported in text
direction: copy-paste prompting associated with lower comprehension; code-syntax prompting with highest
independence_flags: none
quality_notes: correlational, exploratory, overlapping categories, tiny cells; 'copy criteria' (0.654) is nearly indistinguishable from the next-lowest strategies; groups differ in BG ability slightly

method: Observational sub-analysis within agent arm (n=27); review behaviour logged from UI
population: 27 agent-arm students (subset of the n=54 study)
metric: Mean comprehension by review behaviour; regression with BG control
effect_size: Mean comprehension: auto-accept 0.615 (n=6), override changes 0.661 (n=15), Accept All 0.664 (n=20), Accept each file 0.777 (n=7); even reviewers-of-each-file below chatbot mean (per text; group mean not given); regression (BG-controlled) coefficients: auto-accept -0.3343, override -0.2136, accept-all -0.1585, no CIs or p in text
direction: passive acceptance associated with lower comprehension; careful file-by-file review with highest but still below chatbot
seniority_split: not split; per-file reviewers also had higher BG (0.714 vs 0.603 for auto-accept)
independence_flags: none
quality_notes: correlational; n=6 and n=7 cells; BG ability confounds (auto-accept group lowest BG 0.603); categories overlap

method: Post-task Likert (1-5) self-report, mean+/-SE, n=27 per arm; no significance tests reported in text
population: n=54 CS students (17 BSc/31 MSc/11 PhD recruited n=59, 5 dropped) at two US colleges; 27 per arm; mean 5.4 yrs coding, 16.2 months AI use; no professionals
metric: Self-reported helpfulness, effort, and preference
effect_size: Helpful: agent 4.7+/-0.2 vs chatbot 3.3+/-0.2; mental effort: 1.9+/-0.2 vs 3.7+/-0.2; prefer agent for new tasks: 4.2+/-0.2 (agent arm) vs 3.9+/-0.2 (chatbot arm); prefer switching between tools: 4.6+/-0.2 vs 4.1+/-0.3; 'prefer chatbot' 3.2+/-0.3 (agent arm) vs 2.7+/-0.2
direction: agent perceived more helpful, less effortful, and preferred
independence_flags: none
quality_notes: preference measured after one short session; users in each arm only experienced their own tool (the chatbot arm used the agent never, agent arm used chatbot only in the extension warm-up/task) so preference ratings are partly hypothetical

method: Paired self-report vs measured; Likert 1-5 plus measured comprehension; Appendix A.6 regression of perceived on measured (values in Table 8, not read)
population: n=54 CS students (17 BSc/31 MSc/11 PhD recruited n=59, 5 dropped) at two US colleges; 27 per arm; mean 5.4 yrs coding, 16.2 months AI use; no professionals
metric: Perceived understanding vs measured comprehension; preference vs understanding
effect_size: Self-reported 'I understand how my code works': agent 3.3+/-0.3 vs chatbot 4.2+/-0.2 (gap 0.9 points on 5-point scale, same direction as measured comprehension gap d>0.80); 'code feels like my own' 2.5+/-0.2 vs 3.7+/-0.2; 'could easily extend' 3.1+/-0.3 vs 3.2+/-0.2; NO perception-reality gap in direction: agent users correctly rated their understanding as lower, yet still preferred the agent (4.2 vs chatbot-arm 3.9); Appendix A.6: perceptions positively and significantly correlated with measured comprehension and extension accuracy
direction: perception tracked reality (users knew they understood less) but preference followed speed and ease
independence_flags: none
quality_notes: CONTRASTS with the METR-style overestimation pattern: here users were calibrated on understanding; delta is between preference and understanding, not between perceived and measured; no formal test of the delta in text

method: Study design and scope record: randomised between-subjects, exploratory analyses, in-progress preprint (arXiv v1, 29 Jul 2026, cs.CL/cs.HC), n=27 per arm
population: n=54 CS students (17 BSc/31 MSc/11 PhD recruited n=59, 5 dropped) at two US colleges; 27 per arm; mean 5.4 yrs coding, 16.2 months AI use; no professionals
metric: Design, population and generalisability
effect_size: Authors state findings 'may not apply to other user groups and tasks'; sample 'moderate, so all analyses are exploratory'; no professional developers; two website tasks (stated) though one initial plus one extension task reported; agent is Aider with diff accept/reject in a custom VibeJam IDE, not Cursor or Claude Code; authors explicitly decline to claim transfer, only citing Kam et al. 2025 that many professionals value understanding
codebase_context: greenfield single small task, about 70 min total, one session, no longitudinal follow-up
independence_flags: NSF grants iis-2339746, iis-2403436, dge-2236417; University of Maryland, NYU, CMU authors; students received course credit; Gemini and GPT used as judges and question generators
quality_notes: do not cite as professional-developer evidence; mechanism and design-recommendation value only; effect on skill retention over weeks untested

method: Matched event study (generalised DiD) on GitHub public-repo telemetry; adopter matched 1:1 to a non-adopter observed the same calendar week one year earlier; matching on 11-week pre-adoption commits; weeks 21-30 post-adoption bin; SEs clustered by developer
population: Copilot autocomplete subscribers who subscribed in 2022; 15,328 matched adopters (of 397,586 subscribers), 14,279 matched pairs in commits regression; Microsoft subscription dates
metric: Weekly commits per developer, % change vs own pre-adoption mean (weeks 21-30)
effect_size: +30.2% (SE 2.7); weeks 1-10 +44.1 (SE 2.6), weeks 11-20 +28.3 (SE 2.5); matches Cui et al. 2026 field-experiment +26% (SE 10%) per the authors
seniority_split: No seniority or tenure split; only split is pre-adoption activity quartile; effect larger for less active developers: Q1 +61%, Q4 +20%
codebase_context: Public GitHub repositories only (open source; little enterprise coverage); not task-typed
independence_flags: Adoption dates for autocomplete/GitHub Sync from confidential Microsoft telemetry; two of three authors are paid Microsoft research consultants and former Microsoft postdocs (NBER disclosure); working paper, not peer-reviewed; observational
quality_notes: Activity metric (commits) not output value; pre-trends flat; Docker placebo settles ~+7%, GitHubPro placebo ~0; commit size did not shrink; bug-fix share stable (see quality row)

method: Matched event study (generalised DiD) on GitHub public-repo telemetry; adopter matched 1:1 to a non-adopter observed the same calendar week one year earlier; matching on 11-week pre-adoption commits; weeks 21-30 post-adoption bin; SEs clustered by developer
population: Pooled sync-agent adopters (Claude Code via CLAUDE.md commit, GitHub Copilot agent mode via Microsoft usage, plus human-authored activity of Codex and GitHub Agent adopters); 140,118 matched pairs in commits regression; adoption Feb-Nov/Dec 2025
metric: Weekly commits per developer (human-authored), % change vs own pre-adoption mean (weeks 21-30)
effect_size: +153.2% (SE 2.7); weeks 1-10 +81.3 (SE 1.9), weeks 11-20 +98.5 (SE 2.0); by tool weeks 21-30: Claude Code +295.5 (SE 7.7), GitHub Sync +126.3 (SE 3.2), OpenAI Codex +118.8 (SE 4.6)
seniority_split: No seniority or tenure split; only split is pre-adoption activity quartile; Q1 +345%, Q2 +163%, Q3 +90%, Q4 +53% (commits, by pre-adoption activity)
codebase_context: Public GitHub repositories only (open source; little enterprise coverage); not task-typed; sync/async attribution blurred because most sync tools can run async and async adopters also use sync mode
independence_flags: Adoption identified from traces (CLAUDE.md file) and Microsoft usage; Claude Code adopters are early adopters so tool differences may be selection; Adoption dates for autocomplete/GitHub Sync from confidential Microsoft telemetry; two of three authors are paid Microsoft research consultants and former Microsoft postdocs (NBER disclosure); working paper, not peer-reviewed; observational
quality_notes: Authors show effect rises with calendar time in a fixed early-adopter Claude Code cohort and aligns with Opus 4 to 4.5 releases (model improvement, not learning, drives growth); first-week spike excluded (+236%)

method: Interrupted time series on agent-authored commits (no control counterfactual) on GitHub public-repo telemetry; adopter matched 1:1 to a non-adopter observed the same calendar week one year earlier; matching on 11-week pre-adoption commits; weeks 21-30 post-adoption bin; SEs clustered by developer
population: Async-agent adopters (GitHub Copilot coding agent via copilot-swe-agent[bot] PRs; OpenAI Codex via codex/ branches); pooled; 114,104 pairs in commits regression; adoption May-Dec 2025
metric: Agent-authored commits, as % of developer's own pre-adoption total commits (weeks 21-30)
seniority_split: No seniority or tenure split; only split is pre-adoption activity quartile; agent PR commits Q1 +179%, Q2 +42%, Q3 +22%, Q4 +13%
codebase_context: Public GitHub repositories only (open source; little enterprise coverage); not task-typed; adoption observable only for developers who use the agent on public repos (the authors' internal data: 24.2% of async users identified, 72.9% of their activity public)
independence_flags: Agent-authored output is zero before adoption by definition, so no counterfactual comparison; effect is additive agent commits, not net productivity; Adoption dates for autocomplete/GitHub Sync from confidential Microsoft telemetry; two of three authors are paid Microsoft research consultants and former Microsoft postdocs (NBER disclosure); working paper, not peer-reviewed; observational
quality_notes: Effect decays from initial spike then stabilises; agent commits counted regardless of whether merged or reviewed

method: Sum of the three marginal Table 5/6 effects (reconstruction: 30.2+153.2+60.7; arithmetic matches Figure 1 labels, but the paper text does not state the additive construction)
population: As above, pooled across generations
metric: Cumulative commits effect (Figure 1 and abstract)
effect_size: Autocomplete +30%; plus sync approx +180% (3.4x at async); plus async approx +240% (3.4x); no CI on the cumulative figures themselves, only on components
independence_flags: Adoption dates for autocomplete/GitHub Sync from confidential Microsoft telemetry; two of three authors are paid Microsoft research consultants and former Microsoft postdocs (NBER disclosure); working paper, not peer-reviewed; observational; cumulative figure adds estimates from different cohorts/periods and is not an estimate for any single developer
quality_notes: Must not be quoted as an E3 headline without noting that the first 30 points are E1; sync+async cannot be cleanly separated by the authors

method: Matched event study (generalised DiD) on GitHub public-repo telemetry; adopter matched 1:1 to a non-adopter observed the same calendar week one year earlier; matching on 11-week pre-adoption commits; weeks 21-30 post-adoption bin; SEs clustered by developer
population: Autocomplete adopters; 14,190-14,279 pairs (releases 1,609 pairs)
metric: Attenuation chain, weeks 21-30, % change: lines changed, files, commits, PRs, repos touched, releases
effect_size: Lines +234.3 (SE 17.9); files +50.0 (4.2); commits +30.2 (2.7); PRs +18.3 (2.2); repos +11.9 (1.5); releases +9.0 (SE 5.0, not significant at 5%)

codebase_context: Public GitHub repositories only (open source; little enterprise coverage); not task-typed
independence_flags: Adoption dates for autocomplete/GitHub Sync from confidential Microsoft telemetry; two of three authors are paid Microsoft research consultants and former Microsoft postdocs (NBER disclosure); working paper, not peer-reviewed; observational
quality_notes: Release is a GitHub release object (see notes); releases are rare so the autocomplete release estimate is imprecise

method: Matched event study (generalised DiD) on GitHub public-repo telemetry; adopter matched 1:1 to a non-adopter observed the same calendar week one year earlier; matching on 11-week pre-adoption commits; weeks 21-30 post-adoption bin; SEs clustered by developer
population: Pooled sync adopters; 137,727-140,118 pairs (releases 8,912 pairs)
metric: Attenuation chain, weeks 21-30, % change
effect_size: Lines +957.5 (SE 23.2); files +265.0 (4.7); commits +153.2 (2.7); PRs +86.0 (2.1); repos +47.3 (0.9); releases +19.8 (SE 2.9). Claude Code releases +39.4 (6.8); GitHub Sync +17.3 (3.8); Codex +5.2 (5.5, n.s.)
seniority_split: No seniority or tenure split; only split is pre-adoption activity quartile
codebase_context: Public GitHub repositories only (open source; little enterprise coverage); not task-typed
independence_flags: Adoption dates for autocomplete/GitHub Sync from confidential Microsoft telemetry; two of three authors are paid Microsoft research consultants and former Microsoft postdocs (NBER disclosure); working paper, not peer-reviewed; observational
quality_notes: Releases measured at repository level; release effect builds gradually, no discontinuity at adoption; lag between writing and shipping not modelled beyond 30 weeks

method: Interrupted time series on agent-authored activity (no control counterfactual) on GitHub public-repo telemetry; adopter matched 1:1 to a non-adopter observed the same calendar week one year earlier; matching on 11-week pre-adoption commits; weeks 21-30 post-adoption bin; SEs clustered by developer
population: Pooled async adopters; 111,985-114,104 pairs
metric: Attenuation chain, weeks 21-30, % change (agent-authored)
effect_size: Lines +1254.9 (SE 75.3); files +83.3 (3.5); commits +60.7 (2.4); PRs +68.5 (3.4); repos +19.2 (0.3); releases not estimated (cannot split agent from human at repo level)
direction: up; PRs exceed commits because agents open PRs directly
seniority_split: No seniority or tenure split; only split is pre-adoption activity quartile
codebase_context: Public GitHub repositories only (open source; little enterprise coverage); not task-typed
independence_flags: Adoption dates for autocomplete/GitHub Sync from confidential Microsoft telemetry; two of three authors are paid Microsoft research consultants and former Microsoft postdocs (NBER disclosure); working paper, not peer-reviewed; observational
quality_notes: Release effect for async is absent, so the abstract's 30% cumulative release figure contains no async contribution (9.0+19.8 is approx 29%)

method: Sum of marginal Table 6 effects (reconstruction; matches Figure 1 multipliers)
population: As above
metric: Cumulative chain through async (Figure 1 / abstract)
effect_size: Lines 25.5x; files 5.0x; commits 3.4x (+240%); PRs 2.7x; repos/projects 1.8x (+80%); releases 1.3x (+30%, excludes async); no CIs on cumulative values
independence_flags: Adoption dates for autocomplete/GitHub Sync from confidential Microsoft telemetry; two of three authors are paid Microsoft research consultants and former Microsoft postdocs (NBER disclosure); working paper, not peer-reviewed; observational; headline 240 to 80 to 30 mixes a full three-generation commits figure with a two-generation releases figure
quality_notes: Version drift: rev0 (May 2026) reported 180% to 50% to 30%

method: Structural calibration of nested CES hierarchy to the autocomplete attenuation pattern (6 layers, constant parameters; sum of squared log differences)
population: Autocomplete estimates only
metric: Elasticity of substitution between upstream output and human effort
effect_size: 0.23 (output elasticity q=0.76); no standard error or CI reported; Cobb-Douglas alternative loss more than 100x worse; rev0 gave 0.25 (q=0.75)
codebase_context: Model is stylised; the authors say it is not identification of the production function
independence_flags: Model-dependent and calibrated, not estimated with uncertainty; authors state sync/async layer-specific inputs cannot be separately identified
quality_notes: Treat as illustrative: precision implied by two decimals is not supported by any reported interval

method: Event-study outcomes plus aggregate descriptive series (mechanism tests, 2021-2026)
population: Pooled sync adopters (Table 7A) and releases of adopters' repos (Table 7B)
metric: Experimentation versus scope as drivers of attenuation (weeks 21-30 sync unless stated)
effect_size: Lines added +599.5 (SE 12.3) vs lines deleted +1115.7 (20.5), i.e. 7.0x vs 12.2x; branches created +78.6 (2.4), deleted +109.0 (3.6); lines per commit +67.3 (7.9); files per commit +22.2 (1.3); median lines per release 5.21k (2021) to 13.42k (2026); abandoned-repo share 60.0% (2021) to 69.0% (2026), +3.9pp in 2025 alone
direction: more rework, branching and abandonment; modest growth in release size
seniority_split: No seniority or tenure split; only split is pre-adoption activity quartile
codebase_context: Public GitHub repositories only (open source; little enterprise coverage); not task-typed
independence_flags: Adoption dates for autocomplete/GitHub Sync from confidential Microsoft telemetry; two of three authors are paid Microsoft research consultants and former Microsoft postdocs (NBER disclosure); working paper, not peer-reviewed; observational
quality_notes: Authors conclude scope explains a small fraction and experimentation most of the attenuation; abandonment is not shown to be low quality

method: Descriptive aggregate series from four marketplaces (Apple App Store, Google Play, Chrome Web Store, SourceForge), licensed SimilarWeb and chrome-stats data, to Aug 2026
population: Marketplace app catalogues; non-incumbent app cohorts by first-seen month
metric: New app releases per month (agentic era from Feb 2025)
effect_size: iOS about 33,000-45,000 per month (2023-early 2025) to about 108,000 by April 2026; Google Play from about 42,000 (Jan 2025) to about 99,000 by mid-2026; Chrome extensions rising roughly 7-fold since 2023; SourceForge slight increase; no regression, no CIs
independence_flags: Descriptive, not causal: coincides with agentic tools but is not attributed by design; Authors with Microsoft ties
quality_notes: Rev0 called this a moderate increase; revised text says sharp increase

method: Descriptive; 3-month usage of each monthly app cohort
population: As above
metric: Total cohort usage of new apps (ratings iOS; installs Android/Chrome) and share of new apps failing to reach an audience
effect_size: Aggregate usage did not rise with entry: iOS cohort ratings roughly stable 2024-2025; Android downloads up only modestly; Chrome downloads fell (already falling). Share failing to reach an audience Jan 2025 to Apr 2026: iOS 78% to 87%; Chrome 19% to 33%; Android 22% to 26%; no CIs
direction: flat usage; rising share of invisible apps
independence_flags: Descriptive; authors cannot separate low quality from demand-side congestion
quality_notes: Alternative explanations stated by the authors; no quality measure of apps

method: Quartile interaction with post-adoption bin (Equation 36); quartiles from average of treated and control pre-period activity
population: Same samples as the commit rows
metric: Heterogeneity by pre-adoption weekly commit activity (weeks 21-30)
effect_size: Autocomplete: Q1 +61%, Q2 +23%, Q3 +18%, Q4 +20%; sync: Q1 +345%, Q2 +163%, Q3 +90%, Q4 +53%; async agent commits: Q1 +179%, Q2 +42%, Q3 +22%, Q4 +13% (quartile SEs not extracted from the figure text)
direction: larger percentage gain for less active developers
seniority_split: Proxy for seniority only (activity); no experience, tenure, language, repo-age or OSS-vs-private heterogeneity reported
independence_flags: Percentage gains from low baselines; the authors caution direction may flip as tools improve
quality_notes: Activity quartile is not seniority; top-decile matching imperfect (pre-trend visible in top two deciles of pooled sync level regressions)

method: Calendar-time cohort analysis (early adopters within 3 weeks of launch)
population: Claude Code GA cohort (22 May 2025 anchor) and 2022 autocomplete cohort
metric: Source of growth in sync effect over event time
effect_size: Claude Code cohort effect declines then stabilises through Opus 4 and 4.1 eras, then rises sharply with Opus 4.5; autocomplete cohort shows no increase in event or calendar time; authors infer growth is driven by model improvement rather than within-developer learning
independence_flags: Visual/descriptive; no quantified test
quality_notes: Era-relevant: effects are not stable parameters across model generations

method: Placebo and robustness checks
population: Docker adopters (n=266,265 matched) and GitHubPro 2022 subscribers (1,050 matched); contemporaneous-control re-estimate
metric: Activity-bias and design checks
effect_size: Docker settles at +6.6% against agent +153.2% (upper bound on activity bias); GitHub Pro about 0; contemporaneous matched controls give estimates smaller by 21% on average; results similar under level regressions and alternative winsorisation/matching windows
independence_flags: Time-shifted design needs no calendar-time shocks after the last adoption (Appendix F); authors choose it because contemporaneous controls are contaminated by private AI use
quality_notes: Controls from the year before: any general shift in commit behaviour between years would load onto treatment

method: Classification of commit messages; commit-size event study; comment-line share of releases
population: Autocomplete and pooled sync samples
metric: Quality/verbosity proxies only
effect_size: Bug-fix share relative to feature commits stable after adoption (Figure OA-16); no decline in commit size (Table 7); comment-line share of releases 18.6% (2021) to 17.4% (2026), no upward trend
quality_notes: Proxies only. ABSENT: defect rates, escaped bugs, incidents, security findings, review time/quality, revert or change-failure rate, maintainability; the authors infer review as the bottleneck from the model, not from review data

method: Descriptive aggregate series (GitHub Search API, claudescode.dev)
population: All public GitHub activity 2019-mid-2026
metric: Platform-level activity
effect_size: Claude-signed commits exceed 7% of public commits by mid-2026 (undercount); merged PRs and new non-fork repos break above linear pre-2025 trend, PR acceleration larger than repo acceleration; GitHub CTO (cited in paper) reports monthly commits 1.4bn to 2.9bn Apr to Aug 2026
independence_flags: Search API counts are sampled estimates; trend extrapolation is visual, no tests
quality_notes: Consistent with attenuation but not a test of it

method: Instrument development and validation (classifier on 441 private repos from 27 orgs; Guttman scalogram; 3-annotator held-out check of 35 repos)
population: 441 corporate repos (27 orgs) development frame; 217 with >=1 validated AI artifact (1,046 artifacts); 35 Study 2 repos human-annotated
metric: RAMP four-level maturity classification: reproduction of human repo-level label
effect_size: 34/35 repos exact match (97.1%; Wilson 95% CI 85-99; cluster-bootstrap 91.4-100); quadratic-weighted kappa 0.829; file-level accuracy 81.7% (Wilson 95% CI 75.3-86.7; cluster-bootstrap 63.3-95.6; n=175); Krippendorff alpha 0.572 (moderate); Guttman CR 0.997, CS 0.983; Loevinger H 0.299; no L4 in the 441 sample (L1 294, L2 109, L3 38)
direction: Instrument is valid for L1-vs-L2/L3 separation; skills/flows categories (L3/L4) weakly validated (human support <=5 items)
codebase_context: Detects committed config for 12 tools (Claude Code .claude/ CLAUDE.md, Cursor .cursor/ .cursorrules, Copilot .github/, Windsurf, Aider, AMP, Gemini CLI, IDX, JetBrains AI, Kiro, Codex, OpenHands) plus AGENTS.md/*mcp*.json; presence only, not content quality or enforcement
independence_flags: Author overlap: Denisov-Blanch/Schaeffer/Miranda/Koyejo (Stanford) and Agarwal/He/Vasilescu (CMU) are the authors of the re-used panel (Agarwal et al. MSR 2026) and He et al. 2026 benchmark; Grid Dynamics co-author (consultancy); no funding statement; reuses a single dataset so not independent of Agarwal et al.
quality_notes: 97% is 34 of 35 repos with level-stratified sampling (stratum-weighted, not population rate); human agreement only moderate; some cumulative structure imposed by construction (acknowledged); corporate dev sample unidentifiable so not independently checkable

method: Staggered DiD (Borusyak imputation, SE clustered by repo) re-run within maturity strata on Agarwal et al. panel; PS-matched controls (606) shared across strata
population: Agent-first treated repos (OSS): 214 at L1 vs 182 at L2+ (of 396); controls 606; panel to Nov 2025
metric: Monthly commits after first agent-attributed PR, by RAMP stratum
effect_size: L1: beta 0.319 (SE 0.074), +37.56%, p<0.001; L2+: beta 0.243 (SE 0.067), +27.52%, p<0.001; ratio 1.4x. Abstract rounds to 28-38% more commits regardless of maturity
direction: Up in both strata; no velocity penalty for unconfigured repos (L1 nominally larger)
codebase_context: OSS repositories, mixed size/age (median age 553-639 days); not mature enterprise brownfield specifically; commits are a volume proxy
independence_flags: Author overlap: Denisov-Blanch/Schaeffer/Miranda/Koyejo (Stanford) and Agarwal/He/Vasilescu (CMU) are the authors of the re-used panel (Agarwal et al. MSR 2026) and He et al. 2026 benchmark; Grid Dynamics co-author (consultancy); no funding statement; reuses a single dataset so not independent of Agarwal et al.
quality_notes: Commit count is activity not delivered value; commits may rise because agents commit more granularly; L1 vs L2+ difference in commits not tested for significance

method: Same stratified staggered DiD; SonarQube cognitive complexity (log outcome)
population: Agent-first: 214 L1 vs 182 L2+; shared 606 controls
metric: Change in cognitive complexity after agent adoption, by RAMP stratum
effect_size: L1: beta 0.423 (SE 0.118), +52.70%, p<0.001; L2+: beta 0.236 (SE 0.077), +26.68%, p<0.01; ratio 2.0x. Event-study pre-trends small for complexity in both strata. Agarwal et al. pooled average was +39% (He et al. Cursor benchmark +41%)
direction: Complexity rises in both strata; roughly twice as much without committed config; significant +26.7% persists even with config
codebase_context: OSS; SonarQube static proxy; panel window to Nov 2025, event study +/-6 months
independence_flags: Author overlap: Denisov-Blanch/Schaeffer/Miranda/Koyejo (Stanford) and Agarwal/He/Vasilescu (CMU) are the authors of the re-used panel (Agarwal et al. MSR 2026) and He et al. 2026 benchmark; Grid Dynamics co-author (consultancy); no funding statement; reuses a single dataset so not independent of Agarwal et al.
quality_notes: Better identified than warnings; gap widens through month 6, no reversion seen; L2+ labels assigned from end-of-window snapshot and only 3.8% of agent-first L2+ repos committed config before the adoption month (reverse causality/timing); static metric not defects

method: Same stratified staggered DiD; SonarQube static-analysis warnings (log outcome)
population: Agent-first: 214 L1 vs 182 L2+; shared 606 controls
metric: Change in static-analysis warnings after agent adoption, by RAMP stratum
effect_size: L1: beta 0.216 (SE 0.077), +24.08%, p<0.01; L2+: beta 0.131 (SE 0.066), +14.04%, p<0.05; ratio 1.7x. L1 below He et al. Cursor benchmark of +30%; L2+ well below
direction: Warnings rise in both strata; 1.7x larger without committed config
independence_flags: Author overlap: Denisov-Blanch/Schaeffer/Miranda/Koyejo (Stanford) and Agarwal/He/Vasilescu (CMU) are the authors of the re-used panel (Agarwal et al. MSR 2026) and He et al. 2026 benchmark; Grid Dynamics co-author (consultancy); no funding statement; reuses a single dataset so not independent of Agarwal et al.
quality_notes: Authors state warnings are more weakly identified: L1 shows elevated PRE-treatment coefficients (parallel trends doubtful); the two strata's CIs likely overlap (betas 0.216 vs 0.131, SEs ~0.07); no test of between-stratum difference reported

method: Robustness: four-level gradient and boundary sensitivity (pooled agent-first plus IDE-first sample)
population: 509 classified treated repos: L1 236, L2 210, L3 23, L4 40 (agent-first 214/155/5/22; IDE-first 22/55/18/18)
metric: Cognitive complexity, warnings, duplication by RAMP level (dose-response across levels)
effect_size: Complexity: L1 +54.4%, L2 +39.8% (both p<0.001), L3-L4 indistinguishable from zero. Warnings: L1 +23.0%, L2 +16.7%, non-significant above. Duplication significant only at L1 among L1-L3 but L4 +31.4% (p<0.01), the only significant L4 quality effect. Combined L1-2 group: complexity +46.6%, warnings +20.9% (both p<0.001). Pooled L1 vs L2+: complexity +54.4% vs +35.9% (1.5x), warnings +23.0% vs +20.0%
direction: Monotonic decline with maturity for complexity/warnings; L4 duplication a partial exception (authors read as treatment dose); dominant gap at exit from L1
codebase_context: OSS; L3 (23) and L4 (40) strata small; IDE-first L1 only 22 repos
independence_flags: Author overlap: Denisov-Blanch/Schaeffer/Miranda/Koyejo (Stanford) and Agarwal/He/Vasilescu (CMU) are the authors of the re-used panel (Agarwal et al. MSR 2026) and He et al. 2026 benchmark; Grid Dynamics co-author (consultancy); no funding statement; reuses a single dataset so not independent of Agarwal et al.
quality_notes: Null at L3-L4 may reflect low power (small N) not absence of effect; IDE-first L1 too small to identify; pooling dilutes the gradient so only agent-first stratum supports the headline; L4 repos probably heaviest agent users (dose confound)

method: Study 2 velocity contrast on lines added (same DiD)
population: Agent-first: 214 L1 vs 182 L2+
metric: Lines of code added after agent adoption, by RAMP stratum
effect_size: L1: beta 0.393 (SE 0.191), +48.07%, p<0.05; L2+: beta 0.523 (SE 0.133), +68.72%, p<0.001; ratio 0.7x. Comment line density n.s. in both (+7.07% L1, +1.91% L2+); duplicated line density +15.4% (L1, p<0.05) vs +14.2% (L2+, p<0.01), ratio 1.1x in agent-first
direction: Lines added higher with config (authors: structured repos convert agent activity into more code); duplication contrast absent within agent-first
independence_flags: Author overlap: Denisov-Blanch/Schaeffer/Miranda/Koyejo (Stanford) and Agarwal/He/Vasilescu (CMU) are the authors of the re-used panel (Agarwal et al. MSR 2026) and He et al. 2026 benchmark; Grid Dynamics co-author (consultancy); no funding statement; reuses a single dataset so not independent of Agarwal et al.
quality_notes: Lines added is a gameable volume metric (PROTOCOL §5.7); null duplication contrast within agent-first reported honestly but appears only in pooled sample (+5.9% n.s. vs +16.0%)

method: Study 1: Kaplan-Meier adoption dynamics from git history (Jan 2025-Feb 2026, ~14 months) on the 196-repo temporal subset of 441
population: 196 adopters (of 441 corporate repos, 27 orgs); 404 at risk L1->L2 with 191 events; 191 at risk L2->L3 with 18 events
metric: Lifecycle of committed AI configuration artifacts
effect_size: 73.8% of artifacts committed once and never modified; 95.9% of adopters enter at L2; 83.1% introduce artifacts at exactly one level, 14.9% progress L2->L3, 2.1% inverted; reversals 0%, abandonment 0.5%; median >=441 days (633 days among 87% with pre-adoption history) to first artifact; L2->L3 median 154 days (n=18); maintenance scales with maturity only until artifact count controlled (partial rho -0.072, p=0.32); L3 repos mean 3.4 contributors to AI artifacts vs 1.0-1.5 at L1-L2
direction: Adoption cumulative, forward-only, set-and-forget; maturity is a stable repo property (justifies snapshot use)
codebase_context: Corporate private repos from volunteering orgs; Jan 2025-Feb 2026 window (L1 durations are lower bounds)
independence_flags: Author overlap: Denisov-Blanch/Schaeffer/Miranda/Koyejo (Stanford) and Agarwal/He/Vasilescu (CMU) are the authors of the re-used panel (Agarwal et al. MSR 2026) and He et al. 2026 benchmark; Grid Dynamics co-author (consultancy); no funding statement; reuses a single dataset so not independent of Agarwal et al.
quality_notes: Short window and right-censoring; 27 volunteering orgs, a few large ones could make structure reflect policy; set-and-forget implies stale rules files rather than stewardship; corporate data unidentifiable and unreplicable except via pipeline

method: Authors' own stated limitations and framing (Sections 5.2, 7.2, Abstract)
population: Study 2 strata as above
metric: Causal status of maturity-outcome association
effect_size: Authors: 'Because maturity is observational, correlated engineering discipline or model capability may explain part of the gap; we present these findings as hypothesis-generating'. Maturity assigned from Nov 2025 snapshot; only 11.0% of 273 L2+ treated repos (3.8% in agent-first) committed config before adoption month; L2+ repos pre-adoption: median stars 174 vs 55, PRs 389 vs 87, forks 38 vs 10
direction: Association only; estimates describe heterogeneity in the adoption effect, not a causal effect of maturity (authors' wording)
codebase_context: OSS; strata share control pool so within-stratum balance not guaranteed
independence_flags: Author overlap: Denisov-Blanch/Schaeffer/Miranda/Koyejo (Stanford) and Agarwal/He/Vasilescu (CMU) are the authors of the re-used panel (Agarwal et al. MSR 2026) and He et al. 2026 benchmark; Grid Dynamics co-author (consultancy); no funding statement; reuses a single dataset so not independent of Agarwal et al.
quality_notes: Treat as hypothesis-generating; self-selection into configuration (bigger, more active repos) and unobserved model capability are unadjusted; commit velocity retains partial rho 0.269 with maturity after artifact-count control

method: Scope check: outcome set is Agarwal et al.'s, adopted unchanged
population: Study 2 panel
metric: Defect, review, incident, delivery-stability and cost outcomes
effect_size: Absent: no defect rates, bug/incident data, review burden, merge/rework, DORA metrics, or cost (token/licence/time) data. Quality is measured solely by four SonarQube static metrics (authors: 'proxies rather than direct measures of defects or maintainability')
independence_flags: Author overlap: Denisov-Blanch/Schaeffer/Miranda/Koyejo (Stanford) and Agarwal/He/Vasilescu (CMU) are the authors of the re-used panel (Agarwal et al. MSR 2026) and He et al. 2026 benchmark; Grid Dynamics co-author (consultancy); no funding statement; reuses a single dataset so not independent of Agarwal et al.
quality_notes: Cannot support RQ4 cost profile or RQ5(b) production stability; static proxies only; agent-generated code may differ stylistically in ways that inflate apparent complexity

method: Cross-sectional survey (Aug 2024, Microsoft Forms) plus interviews and observation; SPACE-mapped Likert items
population: 530 responses from 3,500 invited (15% response); over 80% Microsoft US individual contributors (random pool), remainder from 15+ other firms recruited via networks; 10 developer + 20 engineering-lead interviews; 23 experienced Java developers observed with GitHub Copilot
metric: Study design and sample
effect_size: N=530 of 3,500 (15%); analysis restricted to the ~75% who regularly use AI (n~380 for usage-frequency groups); no inferential tests reported except a statement that frequency differences are not significant
measurement_basis: self-reported (survey and interviews); observation qualitative only
seniority_split: 7+ years vs first 3 years: 4% less likely to be daily users; no other seniority split
codebase_context: Microsoft internal plus ad hoc external; AI tools not itemised ('broader range'); observation used GitHub Copilot
independence_flags: Vendor authors studying vendor tools on vendor staff; non-random external recruitment; no funding statement; survey of regular users only (selection toward favourable)
quality_notes: Full text read (arXiv v1 PDF). No instrument published; no tool breakdown; extraction of Fig 2 percentages relies on text. Interview and observation sample details thin

method: Survey, 5-point agreement per SPACE item among regular AI users
population: Regular AI users in 2024 survey (~75% of 530, n~380); mostly Microsoft
metric: Perceived productivity: task throughput (Activity), efficiency, value delivery (Performance)
effect_size: Agree or strongly agree: throughput 88%, efficiency 82%, delivering customer or business value 71%; under 3% disagreed on any item; exact n per item not stated
independence_flags: Vendor COI; user-only denominator; Likert agreement not magnitude; no measured counterpart
quality_notes: Agreement shares, not effect sizes; subject to the perception-reality gap (cf. PROTOCOL 5.1) and cannot be used as impact evidence

method: Survey, 5-point agreement
population: Regular AI users, mostly Microsoft (n~380)
metric: Perceived job satisfaction (Satisfaction); would be sad to lose AI
effect_size: 62% agree AI enhances job satisfaction; 80% of regular users would be sad if they could no longer use it; 90% say AI makes them more productive
independence_flags: Vendor COI; user-only denominator; 'sad to lose' conflates habit with value
quality_notes: Satisfaction is the least contested self-report dimension but still perception-only; one of the few places a self-report is arguably the right instrument

method: Survey, 5-point agreement, plus qualitative interviews
population: Regular AI users (n~380); interviews with 20 engineering leads and 10 developers
metric: Perceived collaboration improvement (Collaboration)
effect_size: 48% agree AI improved ability to collaborate (lowest of five dimensions); few disagreed, large neutral share; interviewees report fewer interruptions and richer senior-junior conversation (anecdotal)
codebase_context: Mostly Microsoft; interviewees include non-Microsoft leaders
independence_flags: Vendor COI; the favourable collaboration narrative rests on quotes from a handful of leaders
quality_notes: Weakest SPACE dimension in the data; authors interpret the neutral share as 'evolving', which is interpretation not data; nothing measured on review queues or interruptions

method: Cross-tab of usage frequency against mean agreement 'AI helps me be more productive' (1-5)
population: Regular AI users: daily n=243, weekly n=117, monthly n=16, less than monthly n=4
metric: Moderation of perceived productivity by individual usage frequency
effect_size: Mean agreement: daily 4.47, 1-2 per week 4.07, 1-2 per month 3.50, under monthly 3.25; authors state differences not statistically significant (small groups); direction of causality unresolved
seniority_split: Seniority effect on daily use only 4% (7+ years vs first 3 years)
independence_flags: Vendor COI; reverse causation (those who value AI use it more); n=4 and n=16 cells
quality_notes: Authors themselves disclaim causation and significance; text says 64% use at least weekly but figure counts imply ~64% daily (243 of 380) and ~95% weekly, so text and figure disagree

method: Cross-tab of team AI adoption level against team-productivity agreement and personal-productivity agreement
population: Survey respondents grouped by self-reported share of team using AI (All, Most, Some); group n not reported
metric: Moderation of perceived productivity by team-wide adoption
effect_size: All of team: 94% agree team productive, mean 4.66 personal; Most: 86%, 4.35; Some: 79%, 4.18. Org advocacy: developers who say their organisation actively advocates AI are 7x more likely to be daily users
independence_flags: Vendor COI; group sizes absent; team adoption is self-reported and confounded by team type and task mix; no tests
quality_notes: Correlational; peer-learning mechanism is the authors' interpretation (no data on learning). The 7x adoption figure is an odds-style ratio with no CI or definition

method: Qualitative: open-text responses, interviews, observation of 23 Java developers on common versus exploratory tasks with Copilot
population: Open-text survey responses; 23 experienced Java developers; 30 interviewees
metric: Task-complexity moderation of AI usefulness
effect_size: No numbers. Routine, repetitive tasks: AI works; novel or complex problems: AI struggles. Observed success depended on task complexity, developer skill and AI familiarity; more experienced developers evaluated output better
direction: positive for routine, negative or null for complex
measurement_basis: self-reported (open text); observation qualitative, no timings reported
seniority_split: Experienced developers better at evaluating output and prompting (observed, unquantified)
independence_flags: Vendor COI; no quantified observational results published
quality_notes: Directionally consistent with the greenfield-versus-brownfield tension but entirely qualitative here; use as corroboration only

method: Framework recommendations (authors' prescriptions, not tested)
metric: Measurement and adoption recommendations
effect_size: n/a — framework: measure all five SPACE dimensions not coding speed alone; developers spend only 14% of time coding new features (cited from Kumar et al. 2025); researchers should test causality, task-specific impact and social dynamics; teams: best-practice docs, local champions; organisations: training, policy, tooling
independence_flags: Vendor COI; recommendations untested within this study
quality_notes: Instrument list is generic (no named metrics); explicitly warns the survey does not measure productivity outcomes; supports multi-dimensional measurement incl. satisfaction and collaboration, which self-report alone cannot validate

method: Design and deployment description: single-pass Gemini 2.5 Flash call over merged test-driver and component logs, auto-triggered on integration-test failure in Google's Critique code review; launched May 2025 on all hermetic functional integration test failures during code changes
population: Google engineers; 22,962 distinct code-change authors, 91,130 code changes, 52,635 distinct failing tests, 224,782 executions (reported); seniority not reported
metric: Deployment scale and mode of operation (not an effect)
effect_size: N=224,782 executions on 52,635 distinct tests across 91,130 code changes; median 16 log files and 2,801 log lines per failing test (mean 26 and 11,058); no control arm
cost_data: Mean 110,617 input tokens and 5,962 output tokens per execution; no dollar figure; p50 56 s and p90 346 s to post finding
codebase_context: Google monorepo; hermetic functional integration tests only (performance, security, reliability tests excluded); internal Critique and test infrastructure
independence_flags: Google authors evaluating Google's own tool; no external replication; observational rollout with no A/B arm or counterfactual
quality_notes: Single LLM call with no tools, no code or change-list input and no fix output, so it is log summarisation rather than agentic debugging; E2-equivalent modality (single-pass LLM) despite 2025 deployment

method: Retrospective manual evaluation: 3 expert developers (each 5+ years, integration-test infrastructure team) judged whether Conclusion or any Most Relevant Log Line gave accurate root-cause context; disagreements settled in a meeting
population: 71 randomly selected real integration-test failures from 39 teams; evaluators did not own the failing code
metric: Root-cause diagnosis accuracy (expert-judged)
effect_size: 64 of 71 accurate = 90.14% (N=71; no confidence interval, no inter-rater statistic, no baseline comparator)
codebase_context: Google; failures sampled across teams; evaluators from the infrastructure team
independence_flags: Authors' own team-adjacent evaluators; lenient success criterion (any listed log line giving accurate context counts); small N; sampling frame and selection of 'random' not described; no precision or recall
quality_notes: Of the 7 misses, 4 were test-driver logs not saved on driver crash and 3 were component logs not saved on component crash (infrastructure bugs), so none are attributed to model reasoning error by the authors

method: Observational rollout feedback via Critique buttons (Helpful / Not helpful / Please fix) over the deployment period
population: 517 feedback events from 437 distinct developers on 458 code changes (about 0.5% of 91,130 code changes); 30 Not helpful from 28 authors; 51 Helpful from 43 authors
metric: Developer-rated usefulness of findings
effect_size: Not-helpful rate 5.8% (30/517); helpfulness rate 62.96% (51 Helpful vs 30 Not helpful, N=81 author votes); Please fix 436 (84.3%) from 370 reviewers; helpfulness rank #14 of 370 tools (top 3.78%); feedback-rate rank #134 of 370 (0.0023 vs median 0.0012, mean 0.1042)
codebase_context: Google Critique; compared with 370 other Critique tools, mostly deterministic lint, style and test checks, not LLM tools
independence_flags: Self-selected respondents; Google-on-Google
quality_notes: Only 81 of 517 events are the helpful/not-helpful signal and 436 are a different action (reviewer asks author to act); 10% not-helpful internal guideline is the benchmark; authors attribute the 63% vs 90% gap to negativity bias without testing it

method: Semi-structured in-person interviews with developers who had given feedback
population: 11 interviewees (code-change authors and reviewers who clicked Useful, Not useful or Please fix); seniority not reported
metric: Perceived usefulness and workflow fit; anecdotal time saved
effect_size: Qualitative; one interviewee (P-1) recalled the debugging as taking 10-15 minutes versus 'over an hour' for typical issues; no counts of positive versus negative interviewees given
independence_flags: Self-selected from feedback givers; no neutral or non-using group; Google-on-Google
quality_notes: Single anecdotal time figure is recollection, not a measurement; developers expect fixes, not only diagnoses (P-3); one found a 'more information is needed' output frustrating (P-9)

method: Latency comparison of tool turnaround against survey-reported manual diagnosis durations; no direct time-to-diagnose or time-to-fix measurement
population: Tool: 224,782 executions; manual-duration baseline: Survey-2, 116 developers (self-reported); EngSat survey 6,059 developers ranked integration-test diagnosis a top-5 complaint
metric: Time to produce a diagnosis versus reported manual diagnosis time
effect_size: Tool p50 56 s, p90 346 s to post finding (measured, N=224,782); manual diagnosis 'often more than an hour and sometimes longer than a day' (self-reported, N=116); no measured time saved, no counterfactual
measurement_basis: both (tool latency measured; manual baseline self-reported)
cost_data: Tool latency and token figures only; no human time or cost-per-diagnosis comparison
independence_flags: Google-on-Google; manual baseline is survey recall
quality_notes: Compares a machine latency to human recall of the whole diagnosis episode; says nothing about whether developers reached a fix faster; the paper claims 'significantly faster' without an experimental comparison; do not cite as a productivity gain

method: Failure-mode and negative-result observations from manual evaluation, deployment and interviews
population: 7 of 71 evaluated failures judged not accurately diagnosed; approximately 20 deployed diagnoses returned 'more information is needed'
metric: Failure modes and non-diagnoses
effect_size: 7/71 = 9.86% misses (all traced to missing logs from infrastructure bugs); about 20 'more information is needed' outputs to date (denominator not given)
independence_flags: Google-on-Google; authors' own investigation
quality_notes: Prompt forbids guessing when the failing component's logs are absent, so missing-log cases abstain by design; no hallucination rate reported; recovered ERROR-level noise acknowledged as misleading but no fix evaluated; no per-failure-class breakdown; developers 'highly sensitive' to unhelpful automatic findings

method: Authors' stated threats to validity and generalisability
population: n/a
metric: Limitations and external validity
effect_size: n/a (qualitative)
codebase_context: Single company, internal infrastructure; one model (Gemini 2.5 Flash, temperature 0.1, top-p 0.8, not fine-tuned), one prompt; model may have drifted during study; log quality varies by component
independence_flags: Google authors; no external review of data; deployment duration not stated beyond launch in May 2025
quality_notes: arXiv HTML render shows unfilled template placeholders for most numbers (figures here are from the PDF); no precision/recall, failure-class breakdown, hallucination audit, ablation or non-LLM log baseline

method: Mining-software-repositories dataset construction: explicit Git-metadata attribution (bot actor logins, AI author emails/names, Co-authored-by trailers) via GH Archive PushEvents Jan 2024-Oct 2025 plus API scan, full-history clone
population: 302,579 AI-attributed commits in 6,299 public GitHub repos (100+ stars; Py/JS/TS production files); Claude 138,249 (45.7%), Copilot 118,012 (39.0%), Cursor 19,587, Devin 14,302, Gemini 12,429
metric: Attribution precision (manual check of random sample)
effect_size: 99.0% conservative (99/100; 100% of 99 verifiable commits); 29 AI tools traced, 5 analysed (more than 10,000 commits each); Codex and Aider not among the five
codebase_context: Public star-filtered open-source repos only; only commits that self-label AI use; mixed human/AI commits possible
independence_flags: Self-built corpus; AIDev not cited and overlap untested; no funding statement; same-group prior work cited
quality_notes: Validates that a trace exists, not that AI wrote the changed lines; per-commit modality (agent vs inline) not separated so E3 tag is predominant not exact; v2 numbers differ from v1 (304,362 commits, 6,275 repos)

method: Differential static analysis (ESLint, Pylint, Semgrep) on parent vs commit versions; issue counted if new on changed lines; NO human-commit baseline
population: 302,579 AI-attributed commits, 6,299 repos
metric: Share of AI-attributed commits introducing at least one static-analysis issue (pooled)
effect_size: 9.1% (27,677 of 302,579 commits); 484,366 issues in 3,946 repos (62.6% of repos)
direction: negative (AI-attributed commits add lint/Semgrep findings) but uninterpretable as AI-vs-human without baseline
codebase_context: Mixed OSS repos, 100+ stars; Py/JS/TS production files; no maturity or review split
independence_flags: No comparison group; static-analysis proxy not defects; ~14% false-positive issues in authors' validation (precision 85.9%, n=99)
quality_notes: Pooled 9.1% conflicts with abstract's 'more than 15% per tool' (per-tool minimum is 17.4%); denominators differ and are not reconciled

method: Issue-type breakdown of introduced issues (ESLint/Pylint smells and correctness; Semgrep security)
population: 484,366 introduced issues: 25,740 / 1,650 / 5,142 commits for smells / correctness / security
metric: Composition of introduced issues by type
effect_size: Code smells 432,748 (89.3%); correctness 28,931 (6.0%; undefined variable/reference 23,856); security 22,687 (4.7%; path traversal 8,677, unsafe format string 4,792)
codebase_context: Python rules dominated by broad exception handling 14.9%; JS/TS by unused variables 13.6%; no severity grading
independence_flags: No baseline; security count mixes exploitable and latent patterns, not separated; severity not reported
quality_notes: Tool-flagged rule hits, not confirmed defects; correctness issues touch only 1,650 commits (0.5% of 302,579)

method: Per-assistant comparison of share of commits with at least one issue and issues per commit (Fig. 7 / Table V; only partly stated in text)
population: Copilot 118,012; Claude 138,249; Cursor 19,587; Devin 14,302; Gemini 12,429 commits
metric: Share of commits introducing at least one issue, by assistant; issues per commit
effect_size: 17.4% (Copilot) to 29.1% (Gemini), all above 15%; issues per commit Claude 1.95 (highest), Devin 0.89 (lowest); other tool values not in extractable text
direction: mixed (all tools introduce issues; ranking confounded)
codebase_context: Tools used in different repos and tasks (Copilot 4,487 repos vs Devin 298)
independence_flags: Authors caution ranking may reflect usage patterns not tools; bulk-generation repos may dominate Claude counts
quality_notes: No baseline; no adjustment for commit size or task; do not use as a tool league table

method: Net-impact analysis: issues introduced vs fixed by the same AI-attributed commits (differential analysis)
population: 302,579 AI-attributed commits, 6,299 repos
metric: Issues fixed minus introduced, by type
effect_size: Smells: 439,817 fixed vs 432,748 introduced (net reduction 7,069); correctness and security: introduced exceed fixed, security about 1.5x as many introduced as fixed (exact fixed counts not in text)
independence_flags: No human comparison; 'fixed' = rule hit absent after commit, may include deletions
quality_notes: Mild null on 'AI only adds debt' for smells; correctness/security direction rests on counts not shown in text

method: Survival analysis: each introduced issue re-checked at repository HEAD (c. Feb-Mar 2026) by rule ID plus code context, renames followed
population: 464,900 tracked AI-introduced issues from 302,532 commits (19,466 of the 484,366 untracked, reason unstated)
metric: Share of AI-introduced issues still present at HEAD
effect_size: 22.7% (105,364 of 464,900); by age cohort: more than 9 months 22.8% (4,893/21,421), 6-9 months 19.4%, 3-6 months 28.2%, less than 3 months 21.3% (no monotonic trend)
direction: negative (non-trivial residual) but no human comparator
codebase_context: Snapshot at HEAD, varying exposure by cohort; no maturity, review or tool splits
independence_flags: v1 reported 24.2%; survival labels 84.8% accurate (n=99, recall 81.2%); deleted/rewritten files count as resolved so persistence may be underestimated; pooled figure dominated by smells (89% of pool), no survival by type
quality_notes: Single snapshot; not a time-to-fix result; 'persist regardless of repo size/popularity' claim has no supporting table

method: Anecdotal fix-latency examples (no distribution)
population: Case examples: Stirling-PDF (Claude), firecrawl (Devin), ArchiveBox (Claude Code), librealsense (Copilot)
metric: Time to fix of selected AI-introduced issues
effect_size: Hours (broad-except), 1 day (unused variable), 3 weeks (undefined constant), 42 days (undefined variable NameError); one Devin no-timeout requests.get from Dec 2024 still unfixed; n=handful, not a distribution
codebase_context: Popular repos (27k-98k stars) with active maintainers
independence_flags: Cherry-picked illustrations; no time-to-fix distribution or fixer identity reported
quality_notes: Do not cite as an effect size; absence of a time-to-fix analysis is itself a gap

method: Authors' stated limitations and absent comparators
population: Same dataset
metric: Presence of human baseline and defect outcomes
effect_size: No human-authored baseline (explicitly declined: untraceable AI use contaminates it); no defect, incident, velocity or severity outcome; Py/JS/TS, 100+-star public repos only
codebase_context: Public OSS; explicit-trace commits only (SATD-like 'visible subset')
independence_flags: Static-analysis proxy for debt; ~14% issue false-positive rate in validation (n=99); architectural, test and documentation debt out of scope
quality_notes: Headline 'more than 15%' is not an AI-penalty estimate; usable as prevalence/persistence signal for RQ3/RQ4 only, not RQ5

method: Sharp-threshold regression discontinuity (ITT, reduced form) on GitHub's undisclosed internal repository ranking for free Copilot access (top-OSS-maintainer programme); linear fit each side; bandwidth +/-100 normalised rank; panel of developer-weeks; all table notes state timeframe Jul 2022-Jul 2023 (one year) although abstract and text describe a 'two year' period (Figure 4 dynamics; full panel of 187,489 developers Jun 2022-Jun 2023 per intro) - internal inconsistency
population: Active maintainers of popular public GitHub repos; 50,032 top developers (2,422,916 developer-weeks) in full sample; 5,521 developers / 215,169 developer-weeks within +/-100 bandwidth; those with Technical Preview Copilot experience excluded
task_types: T4 (nearest fit; coding events on popular OSS repos, not task-typed)
metric: Design validity: first stage and RDD checks
effect_size: First stage within bandwidth: cross-section total Copilot days +6.896 (SE 1.574; baseline 2.146; +321%; F=18.0; N=4,268); ever used +0.061 (SE 0.023; baseline 0.100; +61%; F=17.8); panel days/week +0.125 (SE 0.008; baseline 0.056; +223%; F=435.7; N=215,169); exposure share +0.018 (SE 0.001; baseline 0.008; +214%; F=557.5). McCrary-type density test: coefficient 477.6 (SE 417.2; N=201 rank bins) i.e. no significant bunching. Overall take-up low: 16% of 50,032 ever used Copilot; mean 8.1 days
direction: Eligibility raises Copilot use; no manipulation detected
measurement_basis: measured (Copilot API transactions linked to public activity)
cost_data: None reported (free access for eligible; paid licence USD 10/month or USD 100/year otherwise)
seniority_split: None; ability proxies used only for heterogeneity (see ability row)
codebase_context: Popular, widely used public OSS repositories; maintainers only; public-repo activity only (authors estimate about 50% of activity is private and unobserved)
independence_flags: Co-authors from Microsoft (Peng) and GitHub (Xu); GitHub funded/administered the project and supplied proprietary eligibility and Copilot-usage data; HBS working paper (not peer-reviewed); ITT identification not independently replicable without GitHub data
quality_notes: Threshold is GitHub's own internal ranking cutoff, normalised to zero (not disclosed); treatment is eligibility (ITT) with weak take-up; cross-section first-stage F only 17-18; standard errors described as robust, clustering by developer not stated; covariate smoothness shown graphically (Figure C1); placebo-threshold tests not found in the text read

method: Same RDD, ITT on cumulative share of own activity; Table 2 (bandwidth +/-100)
population: Same as design row; N=269,546 developer-weeks without controls, 248,032 with controls (note: differs from 215,169 stated in Tables 1, A3, C2)
task_types: T4 for coding events (push, fork, pull request, create repository); project management events (issues assigned/closed/labelled/merged/subscribed/reviewed-requested, PR reviews, project boards) have no T-code - proposed taxonomy gap
metric: Coding share of all platform activity (cumulative); project-management share of all platform activity (cumulative)
effect_size: Coding: +0.054 (SE 0.002; baseline 0.434; +12.4%; N=269,546), with controls +0.041 (SE 0.002; baseline 0.457; +9.0%; N=248,032). Project management: -0.100 (SE 0.002; baseline 0.402; -24.9%), with controls -0.089 (SE 0.002; baseline 0.443; -20.1%). Signs inferred from text; minus signs lost in PDF extraction of tables
direction: Shift towards coding, away from project management (activity mix, not volume)
seniority_split: Not split in the headline estimate; see ability row
codebase_context: Popular OSS repos; public activity only
independence_flags: Co-authors from Microsoft (Peng) and GitHub (Xu); GitHub funded/administered the project and supplied proprietary eligibility and Copilot-usage data; HBS working paper (not peer-reviewed); ITT identification not independently replicable without GitHub data
quality_notes: Outcome is the composition of event counts, not output or time; activity types are GitHub event proxies (a push is not a unit of value); shares are cumulative and both outcomes share a denominator that includes residual activity; Table C4 absolute measures coding +94.4 events (SE 22.8) and PM -68.5 (SE 10.8) (signs inferred)

method: Same RDD; robustness of the effort-shift estimate to bandwidth, kernel, and design
population: Same as design row; Table C3 optimal-bandwidth samples N=123,026 / 90,938 (coding) and 132,057 / 95,116 (PM)
metric: Sensitivity of coding and PM share effects
effect_size: Uniform/triangular/Epanechnikov kernels (N=215,169): coding +0.054/+0.052/+0.054 (SE 0.002), PM -0.100/-0.107/-0.110 (SE 0.002). Calonico-Cattaneo-Farrell optimal bandwidth: MSE-optimal (+/-47 coding, +/-51 PM) coding +0.043 (SE 0.002; +9.4%), PM -0.100 (SE 0.002; -28.2%); coverage-error-optimal (+/-35, +/-38) coding +0.023 (SE 0.002; +5.2%), PM -0.051 (SE 0.003; -15.0%). Differences-in-discontinuities: coding +0.032 / +0.030, PM -0.033 / -0.036 (SE 0.001-0.002; PM relative -14.5% / -13.5%). Propensity-score matching: coding +0.038 / +0.042, PM -0.099 / -0.083
direction: Sign stable across specifications; magnitude roughly halves under coverage-error-optimal bandwidth and differences-in-discontinuities
independence_flags: Co-authors from Microsoft (Peng) and GitHub (Xu); GitHub funded/administered the project and supplied proprietary eligibility and Copilot-usage data; HBS working paper (not peer-reviewed); ITT identification not independently replicable without GitHub data
quality_notes: Direction robust, magnitude not: headline 5.4 pp / -10 pp falls to about 2.3 pp / -5.1 pp under the CER bandwidth. Placebo-outcome check (Table C5 residual activity: comment, reaction, starring) reported but values not read. No placebo-threshold test located. Student-access DiD (Table C8 Panel B) gives much smaller effects (about 0.001-0.010 coding)

method: Same RDD; mechanism test 1 (autonomy versus collaboration) via cumulative mean number of distinct collaborators (Table A8) and event-type decomposition (Figure 5)
population: Same as design row; N=161,155 (no controls), 155,113 (controls)
task_types: T4 (coding events); project-management events as above
metric: Distinct collaborators across public repos (cumulative mean); coding by event type (push, fork, PR, create repo); PM by event type
effect_size: Distinct collaborators: -17.251 (SE 0.346; baseline 21.759; -79.3%; N=161,155); with controls -14.697 (SE 0.351; baseline 29.947; -49.1%; N=155,113). Event decomposition (graphical, values not tabulated in text): pushes and repository creation up; forks and PR creation slightly down; closing/merging issues up; review requests, issue assignment, PR reviews, issue subscriptions down
direction: Less collaborative, more independent working; authors read as substituting Copilot for human help
codebase_context: Popular OSS repos; maintainers moving to smaller peer groups ('smaller projects' per authors)
independence_flags: Co-authors from Microsoft (Peng) and GitHub (Xu); GitHub funded/administered the project and supplied proprietary eligibility and Copilot-usage data; HBS working paper (not peer-reviewed); ITT identification not independently replicable without GitHub data
quality_notes: Mechanism is inferred from event types and collaborator counts, not observed directly (Copilot usage content not observed); the 79% fall in peers is a very large effect for a low-take-up ITT and may reflect shifts between repositories or cumulative-measure artefacts; authors do not report a formal mediation test

method: Same RDD; mechanism test 2 (exploration versus exploitation), Table 3
population: Same as design row; N=269,546 / 248,032 (repositories), 181,798 / 170,411 (languages)
task_types: T3 (new repos / new languages as exploratory proxy); not task-typed
metric: Log cumulative exposure to new repositories (exploration) versus previously-touched repositories (exploitation); cumulative distinct programming languages; salary-weighted language exposure
effect_size: New repositories +0.484 log points (SE 0.010; +62.3%; baseline 3.097), with controls +0.367 (SE 0.010; +44.3%).
