Old repositories -0.087 (SE 0.011; -9.1%) / -0.114 (SE 0.011; -12.0%) (signs inferred from text). Language exposure +1.753 (SE 0.075; baseline 9.245; +19.0%) / +1.152 (SE 0.076; baseline 5.127; +22.5%) (text cites 21.8%). Salary-weighted exposure +1.4% (about USD 1,683 on baseline USD 119,371)
direction: More exploration, less exploitation; exposure to higher-paying languages
measurement_basis: measured (platform events; language salary from Stack Overflow 2023 survey)
cost_data: Authors' back-of-envelope: USD 1,683/year labour-market potential minus USD 120 licence = USD 1,563 net; extrapolated to about 300,000 eligible maintainers = about USD 468 million per year (explicitly speculative, no general-equilibrium effects)
independence_flags: Co-authors from Microsoft (Peng) and GitHub (Xu); GitHub funded/administered the project and supplied proprietary eligibility and Copilot-usage data; HBS working paper (not peer-reviewed); ITT identification not independently replicable without GitHub data
quality_notes: Cumulative exposure counts mechanically grow with time and activity; 'exploration' is touching an unfamiliar repository or language, which is not demonstrated value; text and table disagree on language-exposure percentage (21.8% versus 19.0%/22.5%); valuation extrapolation is not evidence

method: Same RDD, heterogeneity by median split on four ability proxies (Table 4, Figure 6); proxies: maximum share of commits across ranked repos (centrality), GitHub achievement badges, follower count, account tenure
population: Same as design row; about 124,000 / 124,000 developer-weeks per half (centrality), 147,814 / 121,732 (achievements), 136,011 / 133,535 (followers), 134,999 / 134,496 (tenure)
metric: Coding-share and PM-share ITT effects, low versus high ability
direction: Below-median 'ability' shifts more towards coding and away from project management; consistent across all four proxies
seniority_split: Ability is proxied by platform prominence and tenure (not skill or output): below-median = less central, fewer achievements, fewer followers, newer accounts. Maps to a junior/low-prominence versus senior/high-prominence axis only loosely; ranking itself explicitly not used as ability
independence_flags: Co-authors from Microsoft (Peng) and GitHub (Xu); GitHub funded/administered the project and supplied proprietary eligibility and Copilot-usage data; HBS working paper (not peer-reviewed); ITT identification not independently replicable without GitHub data
quality_notes: No formal test of the difference between low and high coefficients reported in the text read; proxies are correlated with baseline activity mix (low-centrality baseline PM share 0.432 vs 0.348), so the relative effect may partly reflect different starting points; the shift is in activity composition, not in output gains, so 'benefits more' is the authors' interpretation, not a measured productivity gain

method: Same RDD ITT on quality/ability proxies (Table A7, added in the April 2025 version); no direct output, throughput or defect measure of the developers' own code
population: Individual level N about 248,000-269,000 developer-weeks; repository level N=76,662 / 63,005 (CVEs) and 39,853 / 34,404 (CI, dependency scanning)
metric: Maintainer centrality, achievements, PR acceptance rate; repository critical CVEs, continuous-integration adoption, dependency-scanning adoption
effect_size: PR acceptance rate +0.036 (SE 0.002; baseline 0.765; +4.7%), with controls +0.014 (SE 0.002; +1.9%). Critical CVEs -1.060 (SE 0.305; baseline 7.801; -13.6%) and with controls -1.405 (SE 0.363; baseline 4.218; text states 33.9% lower). Continuous integration +0.038 (SE 0.010; +10.5%) / +0.021 (SE 0.011; +5.4%). Dependency scanning +0.029 (SE 0.010; +5.0%) / +0.005 (SE 0.010; +1.0%). Centrality +0.076 / +0.046; achievements +1.824 / +1.139 (signs partly inferred)
direction: No negative effect on proxies; mostly positive. No measure of speed, throughput or feature output
codebase_context: Popular OSS repos; repository-level security outcomes
independence_flags: Co-authors from Microsoft (Peng) and GitHub (Xu); GitHub funded/administered the project and supplied proprietary eligibility and Copilot-usage data; HBS working paper (not peer-reviewed); ITT identification not independently replicable without GitHub data
quality_notes: These are proxies, not code quality: PR acceptance is gameable and CVE counts depend on disclosure behaviour and repo attention; effect shrinks or vanishes with controls (dependency scanning +1.0% with controls); the 33.9% CVE reduction is a repository-level ITT on a count with high baseline and should not be read as AI-generated code being safer; the paper does not measure productivity, only task allocation

method: Version/recency record: Oct 27 2024 version (HBS WP 25-021 / SSRN 5007084 / CESifo 11479) versus Apr 18 2025 version (full paper read)
population: Not applicable
metric: Version differences
effect_size: Apr 2025 version adds: quality/ability and security proxy table (A7), optimal-bandwidth, kernel, winsorisation, matching and difference-in-discontinuities robustness (C2-C8), absolute measures, 'independent' replaces 'autonomous' wording, and discussion of private-repo underestimation (45.5% of Copilot usage in weeks with no public activity). Whether headline numbers (coding +5.4 pp, PM -10 pp) changed between versions cannot be verified: the Oct 2024 copy obtained is a 24-page extract without the results tables. No journal version or retraction found (one search, Oct 2026)
direction: Qualitative findings identical in both versions as far as text allows; robustness and quality proxies added
independence_flags: Co-authors from Microsoft (Peng) and GitHub (Xu); GitHub funded/administered the project and supplied proprietary eligibility and Copilot-usage data; HBS working paper (not peer-reviewed); ITT identification not independently replicable without GitHub data
quality_notes: Still a working paper 18 months after the April 2025 version; I read the full HBS WP 25-021 (Apr 18 2025, rivista.ai copy of the HBS PDF) plus the 24-page Oct 27 2024 Wharton extract; tables lost minus signs in PDF text extraction so signs are inferred from the authors' text

era: UNSPLIT (no AI-usage variable; E3 modality asserted not measured)
method: Vendor CI telemetry; cross-sectional percentile bands, YoY comparison of Sept 2025 vs (apparently) Sept 2024
population: 28,738,317 CircleCI workflows run 1-28 Sept 2025; projects with >=2 contributors (all time) and workflows run >=5 times in window; thousands of teams (org/project count not stated in extracted text)
metric: Dataset scope for CI-telemetry report
effect_size: n=28,738,317 workflows; 28 days (Sept 2025); prior-year comparison window not stated in the methodology text; industry via Clearbit (partial); default branch = current default (older data may be missed)
codebase_context: CircleCI-hosted projects only; mixed sizes, industries (Clearbit), regions; no codebase maturity data
independence_flags: Vendor (CI platform seller); filters self-chosen; single month so seasonality uncontrolled; no AI variable
quality_notes: One-month snapshot; thousands of teams but unit of analysis (workflow vs project vs org) varies by chart; methodology page is 1 paragraph

method: Vendor CI telemetry; YoY change in mean daily workflow runs
population: All qualifying CircleCI projects (Sept 2025 vs Sept 2024)
metric: Average throughput (number of daily workflows run), all branches
effect_size: +59% YoY (average); same report: median team +4% (4.3% all branches), bottom 25% no measurable change, top 25% +25%, top 10% +47%, top 5% +97% (6.8 to 13.4 daily runs)
independence_flags: Mean-vs-median gap of 59% vs 4% means aggregate is driven by the top tail (top team ~136K runs/day, c.10x the prior leader); throughput = CI runs, not deployments or features; vendor benefits from more pipelines
quality_notes: Workflow count is an activity metric, not delivery; the 59% is mean of a heavy-tailed distribution; do not cite as productivity

method: Vendor CI telemetry; percentile-band YoY change by branch type (median band)
population: Median-throughput CircleCI projects
metric: Change in throughput by branch for the median team: all / feature / main
effect_size: All branches +4.3%; feature branches +15.2%; main branch -6.8% (reported as -7%)
independence_flags: Vendor; AI cause inferred not measured; band is a percentile of the distribution each year (chart title: median teams), not necessarily the same teams tracked
quality_notes: Main-branch decline is the report headline for integration bottleneck; no AI-usage covariate so cannot separate AI from other causes (team churn, CI practice, agent bots)

method: Vendor CI telemetry; percentile-band YoY change by branch type (p90 and p95 bands)
population: Top-10% (p90) and top-5% (p95) throughput CircleCI projects
metric: Change in throughput by branch for p90 and p95 bands
effect_size: p90: all +47.2%, feature +49.3%, main +1.0%. p95: all +96.8%, feature +85.1%, main +26.2%. Report: fewer than 1 in 20 teams absorb AI acceleration without slowing pipelines
direction: p90 main flat; p95 main up
independence_flags: The 1-in-20 figure follows from the chosen p95 cut, not a derived prevalence; Bowley reports the p95 group mean pipeline duration as 6 seconds (not verified in report text I extracted) and one team at ~130K workflows/day can skew aggregates
quality_notes: Cohort selection by throughput rank creates selection and regression effects; main-branch gain +26% still CI runs on default branch, not shipped features

method: Vendor CI telemetry; main-branch workflow success rate time series 2022-2025 (chart; values not recoverable from text)
population: All qualifying CircleCI projects, default branch
metric: Main-branch workflow success rate
effect_size: 70.8% in 2025, lowest in over 5 years (report wording); CircleCI recommended benchmark 90% (stated as CircleCI own guidance, no source given); report reads this as ~30% of merge attempts failing
independence_flags: Benchmark is vendor-asserted; report itself concedes CI failures are not always negative (failing is what CI is for); success rate depends on pipeline design and retry practice; Thoughtworks notes 30% merge-failure reading is an inference
quality_notes: Series charted 2022-2025 only in text I could read; chart data points not extracted; no AI covariate

method: Vendor CI telemetry; median recovery time and workflow duration, YoY
population: All qualifying CircleCI projects
metric: Median MTTR (time to green), workflow duration
effect_size: Typical team MTTR 72 min (+13% YoY); feature-branch MTTR +25% (64 to nearly 80 min); main-branch median MTTR improved slightly to 59.2 min (below 60-min CircleCI benchmark); median workflow duration 2.2 min (2.7 in 2024, -18%); mean 9.9 min (11 in 2024, -10%)
direction: MTTR up overall and on feature branches; main-branch MTTR slightly down; duration down
codebase_context: CircleCI users; main-branch MTTR by company size: 2-5 employees 51.7 min, 21-50 employees 174.4 min, 1000+ 46.5 min (chart labels)
independence_flags: Report headline MTTR rise is all-branch; the main-branch MTTR (the delivery-relevant one) improved, which the narrative downplays; exact MTTR definition (failed to next green) not formally given
quality_notes: Directionally mixed, so the report instability story is partly contradicted by its own main-branch MTTR and duration figures

method: Document analysis of causal framing
population: CircleCI report text
metric: Whether AI usage is measured in the dataset
effect_size: Not measured: no AI-adoption field, tool identifier or agent-authorship flag is described; AI attribution is by assertion, e.g. "Average throughput increased 59% year over year, reflecting a sharp rise in AI-driven code generation" and "driven largely by growing adoption of AI-assisted development and autonomous coding agents"
independence_flags: Vendor sells AI-era CI (autonomous validation); sees pattern as AI-driven without counterfactual
quality_notes: Treat as pattern consistent with a bottleneck displacement hypothesis, not as evidence of AI effect; cannot be an E3 effect-size row

method: Independent practitioner critique of vendor report (blog, 2 Apr 2026)
population: Rob Bowley; reanalysis of published report tables, no new data
metric: Validity of the 1-in-20 and 59% headline claims
effect_size: Argues: throughput = CI pipeline runs/day, not deployments or features; feature-branch throughput effectively meaningless so only main-branch counts (median -7%, p90 +1%, p95 +26%); 1-in-20 claim less solid than it appears (6-second mean duration for that group; one team ~130K workflows/day); integration-bottleneck finding credible
independence_flags: Independent of CircleCI; no new data; I could only read a fetched summary of the post, not verbatim full text
quality_notes: Useful measurement critique for RQ6 anti-metrics (pipeline runs as throughput); not independently verifiable beyond the report tables

method: Vendor PR-level telemetry benchmark (P75 aggregation, anonymised/normalised) plus a separate leadership survey; PR-type labelling method not disclosed
population: 8,109,244 PRs; 4,813 teams; 163,820 active contributors; 42 countries; org mix start-up 59.7% / scale-up 24.4% / enterprise 15.8%; AI-type cut shown Jan-Sep 2025 (overall data window not stated); survey n not stated (percentages imply roughly 94)
metric: Dataset and PR classification definition (agentic AI vs AI-assisted vs unassisted)
effect_size: n/a (descriptive). Definitions as printed: Agentic AI PR = created by an AI agent (Devin, Copilot Coding Agent, OpenAI Codex) that interprets a task, generates code, commits and opens the PR; AI-assisted = human-authored or significantly shaped with AI; Unassisted = authored without substantial AI use. Detection mechanism (bot account, trailer, own classifier) is not stated for any class. Report itself says correlation not causation
codebase_context: Mixed 59.7% start-up skew; no per-class team counts; no repo age or language data
independence_flags: Tier D vendor; sells engineering metrics, AI code review, PR automation and AI governance tooling (reverse-direction COI: a trust gap sells governance); customer self-selection into LinearB
quality_notes: Classification of AI-assisted PRs unverifiable; cannot tell which agentic PRs are non-AI bots (Dependabot etc. are named as earlier non-AI bot examples); no controls for task type; survey-only items are not PR telemetry

method: Cross-sectional PR-level comparison of P75 pickup time by PR type (not within-team over time)
population: Agentic AI PRs vs unassisted PRs vs AI-assisted PRs across 4,813 teams
metric: Pickup time (PR waiting for first reviewer action), P75
effect_size: Report p.18-20: agentic 1,055 min (17.6 h) vs unassisted 201 min (3.35 h) = 5.25x, headlined '5.3x longer'; AI-assisted 496 min (8.3 h) = 2.5x unassisted. Vendor marketing pages disagree with themselves: blog/landing say 'AI PRs wait 4.6x longer before review' (denominator and AI class undefined, not in the PDF) while the chart caption says 5.3x; library page says 5.25x with 17.6 h vs 3.4 h. The 4.6x cannot be reproduced from the PDF
codebase_context: Agentic flows reportedly used for low-priority backlog work and often lack a human owner (report's own explanation); no control for task priority, size or team
independence_flags: Vendor; reverse-direction COI; confounded by ownership and priority per the report itself; cross-sectional
quality_notes: 4.6x vs 5.3x unreconciled by the vendor; P75 only, not median; no CI

method: Cross-sectional PR-level comparison of P75 review time once picked up
population: Agentic vs AI-assisted vs unassisted PRs
metric: Review time P75 (pickup to merge per LinearB definition)
effect_size: Report p.20-21: agentic 382 min (6.4 h); AI-assisted 194 min (3.2 h); unassisted 252 min (4.2 h). So AI-assisted 1.3x faster than unassisted (-23%) but agentic 1.5x SLOWER. The landing-page claim 'reviewed 2x faster once picked up' does not appear in the PDF and contradicts the agentic figure; the report's own text says 'only somewhat slower' for agentic and 'significantly less time' for AI PRs generally
direction: Mixed: AI-assisted faster, agentic slower; vendor interprets as shallower scanning (survey quotes on rubber-stamping)
codebase_context: Review depth not measured; larger diffs reviewed faster is a warning sign not a benefit
independence_flags: Vendor; marketing headline overstates relative to the full report
quality_notes: Faster review is not evidence of efficiency; no post-merge defect linkage

era: E3 (see note: class of 'AI PRs' in the 32.7% headline not specified; benchmark tiers are agentic)
method: Cross-sectional PR-level acceptance (merged within 30 days of creation or leaving draft)
population: Pooled AI PRs vs manual PRs; bot-tool monthly series (Copilot, Devin vs manual) Jan-Sep 2025
metric: Acceptance (merge within 30 days) rate
effect_size: 32.7% AI PRs vs 84.4% manual PRs (p.22). Monthly chart shows manual steady at about 80-82%, so headline manual figure and chart differ slightly; Devin rising from April 2025 towards human baseline, Copilot declining from May 2025 (values read from chart only). Agentic acceptance tiers: elite >71%, good 61-71%, fair 42-60%, needs focus <42%; manual elite >95%; report says most teams find it hard to exceed 60% for AI PRs. Vendor says insight holds at 7d/14d/no-limit thresholds
direction: AI PRs merged far less often
codebase_context: Report attributes gap to missing human owner, low-priority backlog work, larger diffs; PRs younger than 30 days at extraction may be right-censored (not addressed)
independence_flags: Vendor; pooled rate, not per-team; unclear whether denominator includes abandoned bot PRs from non-AI bots or auto-closed PRs
quality_notes: Low acceptance is not evidence of poor quality (ownership and priority confound); no human-owned agentic cohort

method: Cross-sectional PR size distribution
population: Agentic vs AI-assisted vs unassisted PRs
metric: PR size (lines of code), median and P75
effect_size: Median: agentic 89, AI-assisted 96, unassisted 26. P75: agentic 293, AI-assisted 408, unassisted 157. The 408 vs 157 figure (headline '2.6x larger') is AI-ASSISTED vs unassisted, not agentic (agentic is 1.9x at P75). Commit level: AI-assisted commits touch 4.2 files vs 7.51 unassisted, 273 vs 498 average lines, about 65 vs 66 lines per file
direction: AI-involved PRs larger; AI-assisted commits more concentrated
independence_flags: Vendor; commit-level comparison method not stated
quality_notes: Secondary summaries that quote 408 as agentic are wrong

method: Org-level scatter of AI-PR share vs acceptance rate (chart; no numeric deltas in text); vendor narrative
population: Organisations with higher vs lower AI-PR share
metric: Acceptance rate by org-level AI-PR adoption
effect_size: No effect size. Text: orgs with higher AI PR adoption 'rarely outperform' lower-adoption orgs; acceptance shows no meaningful improvement with adoption; one outlier org (Devin, very high adoption) near parity with manual. The widely circulated heavy-adoption figures (+98% PRs merged, +91% review time, +154% PR size) do NOT appear in this report; they appear to be from another vendor's study (my recollection: Faros AI 2025; not verified here)
codebase_context: Selection: orgs choose adoption level; no within-org change over time
independence_flags: Vendor; cross-sectional; not a causal test
quality_notes: 'Heavy adoption' is not defined as a threshold; chart axis values not recoverable from text

method: Not measured in this report
metric: 'Issues per PR' / defect density for AI code
effect_size: Not present. The '1.7x more issues per PR' figure is not in this report (likely from a different vendor's code-review dataset; not verified here). Quality-adjacent measures in the report: refactor rate P75 0.37 unassisted vs 0.22 AI-assisted vs 0.17 agentic; rework rate P75 chart labels 0.05, 0.01, 0.18 (assignment to classes ambiguous; text says agentic shows almost no rework); change failure rate, rework and MTTR are NOT cut by PR type (MTTR removed from benchmarks for definitional variance)
independence_flags: Vendor; reverse-direction COI
quality_notes: Quality of AI code asserted only via survey quotes ('slop', 'rubber stamping') and 39.4% somewhat / 6.4% extremely confident; no incident or defect linkage by PR type

method: Percentile-band benchmark tiers over team-level P75 values
population: 4,813 teams; tiers elite = top 10%, good = top 30%, fair = top 60%, needs focus = bottom 40%
metric: Benchmark tiers: pickup time (all orgs) and cycle time etc.
effect_size: n/a. Pickup time tiers (hours, all orgs): elite <1, good 1-4, fair 5-16, needs focus >16. Cycle time elite <25, good 25-72, fair 73-161, needs focus >161. Review time elite <3, good 3-14, fair 15-24, needs focus >24. PR size elite <100, good 100-155, fair 156-228, needs focus >228. Enterprise/scale-up/start-up bands differ (e.g. enterprise pickup <2 / 2-4 / 5-13 / >13)
independence_flags: Vendor; tiers are relative ranks of customers, not outcome thresholds
quality_notes: Tiers are not validated against delivery or quality outcomes

method: Vendor leadership survey (LinearB users) with adoption, confidence and measurement questions
population: Engineering leaders; n not stated (about 94 inferred from percentage granularity); fielded November 2025
metric: Reported productivity gains vs measurement practice
effect_size: 76.1% of leaders report some (44.6%) or significant (31.5%) measurable improvement in coding speed or output; 44.7% do not measure AI impact formally; confidence in AI code: 6.4% extremely, 39.4% somewhat, 33% neutral, 19.1% somewhat unconfident, 2.1% not at all. Text/chart mismatches inside the report (daily use 64.9% text vs 63.5% chart; 23.4% vs 22.9%; headline '45%/75%' vs 44.7%/76.1%)
independence_flags: Vendor survey; reverse-direction COI
quality_notes: Self-report gains coexist with measured low acceptance and no measured delivery effect

method: Mining study of public GitHub PRs; candidate-fix linking (same repo, merged within 30 days after, fix-type tag, co-edited non-boilerplate file) then 2-annotator + LLM-judge (Claude Opus 4.8) verification of Direct fix
population: 6,774 merged agent PRs (Codex 2,834; Devin 1,813; Copilot 1,428; Cursor 569; Claude Code 130; 891 repos; 24 Dec 2024 to 30 Jul 2025) vs 5,044 merged human PRs (1 Jan to 28 Jun 2025) from AIDev-pop (>=500 stars as of 22 Jun 2025); open-source; no seniority data
metric: Dataset/instrument: post-merge follow-up fix instrumentation on AIDev-pop
effect_size: N=6,774 agent and 5,044 human merged PRs; 4,505 agent PRs fully observed for 30 days; shared-window comparison 2,012 agent vs 4,063 human
codebase_context: Open-source popular repos; agent PRs mostly small; Codex PRs unsigned at commit level
independence_flags: Data is AIDev-pop (Li et al. 2025, another group's corpus; shared provenance and agent-attribution limits with other AIDev studies); funded by Australian Composites Manufacturing CRC grant HPN003; no vendor funding; LLM judge is an Anthropic model while Claude Code is a studied agent
quality_notes: Human PR baseline is not matched on task, size or type; only repository-stratified; Table 3 reports 263 verified pairs but 203 PRs carry a verified fix (pairs vs PRs); preprint v2 24 Sep 2026, journal-targeted (Empirical Software Engineering), not peer-reviewed at time of reading

method: Mantel-Haenszel odds ratio stratified over 218 repositories where both cohorts appear; shared observation window cut at 28 Jun 2025; no PR-size or task-type covariate in this model
population: Merged agent PRs (2,012) vs merged human PRs (4,063) in shared window; AIDev-pop open-source repos
metric: Odds of a verified follow-up fix (Direct fix by a later fix-type PR within 30 days) for agent merges vs human merges
effect_size: OR 1.62 (95% CI 1.10-2.39, p=0.015); candidate-fix OR 1.41 (95% CI 1.19-1.68); verified 3.68% (74/2,012) vs 2.34% (95/4,063); MH risk ratio 1.59; day-30 cumulative incidence 4.5% vs 2.6%
direction: Agent merges more often followed by a fix (higher rework signal for agents)
cost_data: none reported (no time or cost of fixes)
codebase_context: Repo-matched only: 218 strata; human PRs not matched on size/task type; absolute rates are low (about 3-4%)
independence_flags: Same AIDev-pop provenance; CI lower bound close to 1; fix definition requires a fix-type tag and file overlap so both cohorts are floors; agent attribution in AIDev from commit-author patterns
quality_notes: Wide CI; correlational; effect may reflect agent PRs differing in task mix or size; also differential detectability (agent fixes tagged and linked identically but LLM judge developed on agent pairs)

method: Authorship classification of the PR that opened each verified fix (self-agent / other-agent / human), per agent
population: 263 verified fix pairs on agent merges (Codex 125; Devin 88; Copilot 40; Cursor 8; Claude Code 2); 110 verified pairs on human merges
metric: Share of verified fixes on agent merges opened by the same agent
effect_size: 69.6% self-agent, 27.4% human, 3.0% other agent (n=263); Codex 59.2% self / 38.4% human; Devin 72.7% / 23.9%; Copilot 95.0% / 5.0%; Cursor 87.5% self (n=8); Claude Code n=2 uninformative; human merges: 89.1% human-fixed, 10.9% agent (n=110)
direction: Agent merges mostly fixed by the same agent; humans still author about a quarter
codebase_context: Open-source; who invokes the agent to fix is not observed (a human may trigger the agent)
independence_flags: Same AIDev-pop provenance; Codex PRs carry no commit marker; unmarked agent PRs in human table would inflate human-fixed share
quality_notes: Opener identity is not the same as who decided a fix was needed; small n for Cursor and Claude Code; Copilot 95% may reflect Copilot workflow where it iterates on its own PRs

method: Rule-based commit author-class classifier (agent / automation / human) on login and message markers, aggregated per PR; Codex excluded (unsigned)
population: 123 verified-fix agent PRs excluding Codex (Copilot 40; Devin 59; Cursor 23; Claude Code 1) and 124 human-opened fix PRs (554 commits); 3,940 non-Codex merged agent PRs for comparison
metric: Agent-authored share of commits within verified-fix PRs
effect_size: Average 87.4% agent-authored per PR; 76.4% of these PRs are agent-authored throughout all commits (Copilot 86.6/70.0; Devin 92.0/84.7; Cursor 79.1/69.6); human-opened fix PRs 0.8% (n=124); all non-Codex merged agent PRs 78.8% average, 54.1% all-agent
direction: Agent-opened fix PRs are mostly agent-written; higher agent share on fix PRs than on merges generally
independence_flags: Same AIDev-pop provenance; shares are lower bounds because unmarked agent commits count as human; authorship is committer or marker, not who wrote the change
quality_notes: Headline 76.4% is of fix PRs not of all fixes (Codex's 103 fix PRs excluded); conclusion that humans 'retain maintenance' or not is not supported either way (27.4% human-opened)

method: Per-agent verified-fix rates within 30 days of merge (candidate, verified, precision-adjusted)
population: Fully observed agent PRs: Codex 2,049; Devin 1,519; Copilot 721; Cursor 153; Claude Code 63 (of 130; 67 dropped as merged within 30 days of dataset end)
metric: Per-agent share of merges followed by a verified fix
effect_size: Verified rate: Codex 5.5% (adjusted 4.9%); Cursor 5.2% (5.0%); Devin 3.7% (3.4%); Claude Code 3.2% (3.2%); Copilot 3.5% (3.1%); overall 4.5% (adjusted 4.1%, n=203/4,505); candidate overall 22.9% (n=1,032)
direction: Per-agent differences small; no agent comparison tested
independence_flags: Same AIDev-pop provenance; per-agent comparisons not tested and agents work on different task mixes and repos
quality_notes: Claude Code and Cursor n too small for ranking; do not rank agents on this table

method: Validation of fix labelling: two annotators on 50 sampled agent pairs; LLM judge re-validated on 50 agent plus 50 human pairs
population: 50 human-labelled pairs; judge applied to 2,510 agent-merge and 2,206 human-merge candidate pairs
metric: Agreement of verification instrument
effect_size: Human-human binary kappa 0.77 (45/50 agree, 90%); judge-human binary kappa 0.78 (agent pairs); Direct-fix precision 27/30=90% in each cohort, pooled 54/60=90% (Wilson 95% CI 80-95%); three-way kappa 0.60 human-human and 0.46 judge-human
direction: Binary verification reliable; three-way labels unreliable
independence_flags: Annotators are authors (3-4 years' experience); judge developed on 45 agreed pairs from agent cohort; judge is Claude Opus 4.8
quality_notes: Small validation samples (50 pairs); recall of the judge not measured; precision 90% means about 10% of verified fixes are false positives

method: Within-repository conditional logistic regression of verified fix on merge-time signals with PR size (non-boilerplate files shipped) control; plus authors' stated threats to validity
population: Verified-fix vs no-fix agent merges, AIDev-pop
metric: Merge-time predictors of a later fix; limitations
effect_size: Pooled: all effects negligible to small (Cliff delta: time under review -0.221 and review items -0.239 small, p<0.001; commits +0.013 p=0.75; churn +0.032 p=0.41). Within-repo, tenfold more commits: OR 6.1 (p<0.001); review items OR 2.4 (p=0.022); churn OR 1.3 (p<0.001); time under review no effect (p=0.18)
direction: Merges that needed many commits are likelier to need a later fix; less review time/items slightly associated with fixes in pooled view
independence_flags: Same AIDev-pop provenance; severity not measured; 30-day window and file co-location miss cross-file or later fixes (rates are floors)
quality_notes: No severity, no cost; fix = Direct fix by later fix-type PR editing a shared file; scope limited to 5 agents in >=500-star repos; no null-result suppression observed

method: Single-case practitioner-researcher study, within-case descriptive; baseline = same squad's historical BCP throughput (no control)
population: 1 staff engineer (8+ yrs, 4 yrs in stack/domain) + 3 AI tools in 4 roles; Itau Unibanco (Brazilian bank, BACEN/CVM regulated); digital-signature platform, 4 microservices + 1 Angular frontend (9 repos); 5 features / 25 stories; Aug-Sep 2025
metric: Setting and design of single-case one-person AI-augmented squad under Spec-Driven Development
effect_size: n=1 case; 1 engineer; 3 sprints x 3 weeks; no inferential statistics
cost_data: AI tooling est. R$5,000-R$7,000; staffing R$60,000 vs R$492,000 original project cost
seniority_split: 1 staff engineer only; paper cites Cui et al. for junior/senior divergence but does not measure it
codebase_context: Brownfield, production since Oct 2025; system age, LOC, language mix (Kotlin/Java backend, Angular frontend) partly given; pre-existing coverage not reported
independence_flags: First author is the engineer-subject (practitioner-researcher); Itau authors; one co-author (Pinto) co-authored StackSpot paper (Itau platform used); no external audit; code not releasable
quality_notes: Self-authored by participant; outcome metrics said to be pre-defined; managers reviewed data via sprint reporting; artefacts proprietary; NB venue not stated (arXiv preprint, 10 pages, v2)

method: Single case; comparison of actual 3 sprints vs original 6-sprint plan
population: 1 staff engineer vs plan for 4-person squad over 6 sprints (~18 wks); actual 3 sprints (~9 wks)
metric: Delivery time vs plan (time-to-market)
effect_size: -50% (3 sprints/9 weeks vs 6 sprints/~18 weeks); 5 features delivered in 3 sprints; baseline squad 4-5 features per 4 sprints (about 1.0-1.25 features/sprint vs 1.67 actual, ie about 1.3-1.7x per sprint, derived not reported)
measurement_basis: measured (sprint records) against a plan of unstated provenance
codebase_context: Brownfield regulated; Sprint 1 spent on repo scaffolding and infrastructure (7 stories, 0 features, 79 BCP); avg lead time per story 17.6 d (15/20/18) did not fall as throughput rose, authors attribute to homologation windows and sign-offs
independence_flags: Plan estimator not identified; paper alternates between plan and historical baseline as comparator; 'half time' is also half the sprints not half the effort (1 vs 4 people)
quality_notes: Time halved but person-effort comparison is 9 vs 72 person-weeks; ramp-up and spec effort in Sprint 1 included; no estimate of plan accuracy

method: Single case; BCP throughput vs same squad's prior projects
population: 1 engineer, 890 BCP delivered (79/377/434 by sprint); baseline = prior squad velocity on comparable scope
metric: Effort per Business Complexity Point (BCP) vs historical baseline
effect_size: Reported 8.93 h/BCP -> 2.2 h/BCP (-51%); BUT Table II gives 2.20 BCP per engineer-hour (0.46 h/BCP overall; 1.71/0.36/0.31 by sprint) - unit mismatch unresolved; throughput 0.59 -> 3.21 BCP/eng-h S1 to S3 (5.4x)
measurement_basis: measured (BCP assigned by internal AI scoring component, unadjusted) but metric validity weak
codebase_context: Same product domain and codebase as baseline; feature mix differs across cycles (acknowledged); frontend stories score higher and sprint mix shifted to frontend (composition effect acknowledged)
independence_flags: BCP is an institutional proprietary complexity score produced by an AI scorer from story text (CI&T); scored by AI so possible circularity; one-person eng-hours self-recorded
quality_notes: Headline -51% depends on a unit-ambiguous figure; if 0.46 h/BCP were the right comparator reduction would be about 95%, implausible, so treat the baseline as unverified; 8.93 h/BCP x 890 BCP implies about 7,950 baseline hours which looks inconsistent with 4 engineers x 18 weeks

method: Single case; participant-judged acceptance of AI output at first review
population: AI-generated code across 25 stories (Copilot agent mode for core, Devin autonomous for non-core); reviewer = the sole engineer
metric: Share of AI-generated code accepted at first review without structural modification
effect_size: 90% (denominator unit not defined: lines, files, PRs or generations unknown; formatting and naming changes not counted as rejections)
measurement_basis: self-reported (engineer's own acceptance judgement; no independent review; not an automated count)
seniority_split: 1 staff engineer, 8 yrs, deep institutional knowledge
codebase_context: Brownfield with detailed spec supplied; agents given multi-repo context
independence_flags: Reviewer is the author/subject; the acceptance-rate construct is on the protocol anti-metric watch list; no rework hours or review-time data
quality_notes: Acceptance rate is a gameable metric per PROTOCOL 5.7; no measurement of what review caught; threshold leniency (minor edits excluded) unquantified; no breakdown core vs non-core

method: Single case; CI/CD gate outputs plus defect log
population: 113 integration tests (24/37/52), 65 E2E (15/21/29), backend coverage 92.8% avg, frontend 90.3%, 10 manual WCAG sign-offs; AI-generated tests reviewed by engineer
metric: Test coverage, integration/E2E pass rate and defects
effect_size: Integration 113/113 (100%); E2E 65/65; coverage 90.4-95.7% backend, 90.1-90.7% frontend vs 90% gate; defects post-validation 1 (accessibility, Sprint 2), post-release 0
direction: no defects observed (near-null variance by construction)
measurement_basis: measured (pipeline-recorded) but pass rate and coverage are mandatory gates so non-informative about correctness
seniority_split: 1 staff engineer; accessibility judgement by dedicated specialist and homologation team
codebase_context: Production since Oct 2025; post-release observation window not stated; no incident or change-failure data
independence_flags: Authors concede 100% pass reflects the gate not a correctness guarantee; no human-written-test comparison; post-release zero defects has unspecified exposure period
quality_notes: Absence of defects is weakly informative: short window, n=1, no comparison defect rate for the 4-person baseline reported

method: Single case; cost arithmetic by authors
population: Original project cost R$492,000 (4 engineers, 6 sprints) vs actual staffing R$60,000 (1 engineer, 3 sprints)
metric: Direct staffing cost reduction
effect_size: -88% staffing (R$492,000 -> R$60,000); >85% including est. tooling R$5,000-R$7,000 (about -86.4% to -86.8%, derived); consistent with 9 vs 72 person-weeks (-87.5%) if rates are equal (derived)
measurement_basis: self-reported (authors' computation from planned headcount and duration vs actual; 'original project cost' provenance unstated)
cost_data: Tooling R$5,000-R$7,000 estimated, not audited; excludes ramp-up, agent configuration, infrastructure, review/QA/homologation staff outside the squad
codebase_context: As above; homologation, accessibility specialist and managers outside the one-person squad not costed
independence_flags: Cost reduction is mostly plan-to-actual and headcount arithmetic; counted-out roles (homologation team, accessibility specialist, shared platform team) likely not in comparator
quality_notes: Full TCO explicitly not done (authors, Limitations); do not cite as a measured productivity gain; tokens/licence per-seat detail absent

method: Single case; authors' qualitative lessons (retrospective notes and repository history), no instrument
population: Same single engineer and 5 features
metric: Conditions for success: specification quality and institutional knowledge as binding constraints (rather than model capability)
effect_size: Qualitative; no quantified rework or ablation. Claims: vague specs produced 'unusable outputs regardless of tool'; undocumented legacy contracts were the most frequent rework source; core (domain logic) needed human-in-loop, non-core (infra/boilerplate) could run autonomous; Sprint 1 lead time 15-20 d unaffected
measurement_basis: self-reported (participant-authored retrospective; brownfield indicators 'partially reconstructed from retrospective notes')
cost_data: No cost of specification effort quantified apart from noting Sprint 1 spec effort was amortised as reusable prompt material
seniority_split: Single staff engineer; paper argues gains rest on senior expertise (cites Cui et al. and METR from literature, not tested)
codebase_context: Brownfield with documented constraints is enabling; undocumented legacy is limiting (Table VI)
independence_flags: No variation in model, spec quality or engineer tested, so 'binding constraint' is not identified causally; Itau authors benefit from the narrative of institutional knowledge
quality_notes: Plausible mechanism consistent with other practitioner reports but untested; paper itself recommends a two-person pair + fractional product role as more durable and calls it untested

method: Practitioner conference talk (QCon London 2026) plus Q&A; dashboard charts shown; informal counts
population: Duolingo, ~300 engineers, ~200 PRs/day; LLM PR-risk bot with opt-in auto-approval of low-risk PRs
metric: Design of autonomous PR risk-scoring and auto-approval (LLM grades title, verification steps, diff; low/medium/high/undetermined plus explanation)
effect_size: Descriptive: ~10% of all PRs merged via the bot after ~6 months; model/vendor not named
cost_data: None given for bot (no token or licence spend)
seniority_split: Auto-approval restricted to code owners (5-6 per codebase); blocked for new engineers during onboarding; disabled for AWS resource changes and SOX/ISO repos
codebase_context: Single org; ~20-30 contributors per codebase; ~80% of changes in a repo come from owners; project described as vibe coded
independence_flags: Single org; speaker is the builder; no named vendor product for the bot; no independent measurement
quality_notes: Design detail useful for guardrail patterns; model unnamed; transcript fetched via summarising tool so wording is paraphrase-grade

method: Speaker recollection from bucketing research (no method given)
population: Duolingo code changes before the bot
metric: Share of code changes receiving no review feedback
effect_size: 'We have like 30% of our code changes with no feedback' (speaker recollection; no denominator or period)
codebase_context: Duolingo-wide; low-risk bucket correlated with changes already signed off without comments
independence_flags: Single org; basis for the bot's design so motivated reasoning possible
quality_notes: Suggests review effort on trivial changes is substantial; not an audited figure

method: Dashboard time series (median time to merge; bot share of PRs); speaker explicitly calls it a correlation; no control
population: Duolingo PRs org-wide (~200/day)
metric: Median time to merge
effect_size: About 18h to about 12h over about a year while bot-merged share rose ~0% to ~10% over ~6 months (speaker: 'the correlation'; also describes a 'cascading effect' on medium/high-risk PRs)
direction: Decrease in time to merge (association only)
seniority_split: Org-wide; new engineers excluded from auto-approval but included in median
codebase_context: Concurrent AI adoption rising 80% to ~100% is a confound; no pre/post or control group
independence_flags: Same speaker; co-trending confounders (AI adoption, review culture, other tooling)
quality_notes: Correlation only; no causal design; median only, no variance; coincident AI tool adoption not controlled

method: Speaker ballpark in Q&A
population: Duolingo authors offered auto-approval
metric: Share of authors declining auto-approval and requesting human review
effect_size: 'maybe like 20% to 30% is just ballpark numbers'
direction: Mixed: opt-out usage, often cited for mentorship
seniority_split: Opt-in by code owners; others can still request review
independence_flags: Same speaker
quality_notes: Informal; denominator unclear (PRs vs authors); relevant to review-as-mentoring cost

method: Informal count in Q&A
population: Bot-approved PRs at Duolingo (~200 PRs/day overall)
metric: Reverts of bot-approved PRs
effect_size: 'maybe one or two of those are reverts of the auto approve bot requests' per day (informal); speaker says attribution is hard and some reverts are deliberate experiments
direction: No clear direction (no human-reviewed comparison rate)
codebase_context: No comparison revert rate for manually reviewed PRs; some reverts would have occurred anyway
independence_flags: Same speaker
quality_notes: Not a defect-rate measure; no denominator for bot-approved PRs (about 20 per day at 10% share, inferred, not stated); no baseline

method: Audience Q&A answer; no controlled comparison
population: Auto-approved vs manually reviewed PRs at Duolingo
metric: Defect-rate difference between auto-approved and manually reviewed PRs

method: Mining study of 5 OSS agent-harness repos vs 2 baselines (VS Code, GitHub CLI), Mar 2025-Feb 2026; GitHub API

method: Controlled longitudinal benchmark: 35 sequential Qwen Code CLI releases (v0.0.10-v0.10.3, v0.0.11 excluded), fixed self-hosted Qwen3-Next-80B-A3B-Instruct (vLLM 0.18.0), 50 stratified SWE-bench Verified tasks, 2 runs per task (3,500 executions), 600 s timeout
population: Qwen Code CLI on SWE-bench Verified subset (20 easy, 25 medium, 5 hard, 0 very hard)
metric: Resolve rate per release; Spearman trend over release order
effect_size: Mean resolve rate 30.5%; range 23.0% to 39.0% across releases (v0.0.14 peak); Spearman rho=0.208 p=0.231 vs release order (no significant trend); patch produced in 52-94% of tasks; run-to-run 87.7% binary agreement. Reported single-step swings: 39.4% to 32.5% (v0.4.1 to v0.5.0, -6.9pp), 27% to 34% (v0.5.0 to v0.5.1, +7pp, called largest gain), 26.0% to 33.0% (v0.2.3 to v0.3.0). N=35 releases x 50 tasks x 2 runs
direction: Flat on average, large release-to-release volatility (about 16pp envelope); newer releases do not reliably beat early ones
cost_data: Not reported in dollars; see efficiency row
codebase_context: SWE-bench Verified (mostly easy/medium, public repos); not mature proprietary code
independence_flags: Academic; self-hosted model removes silent-model-update confound
quality_notes: 50 tasks gives roughly 1pp per task per run so swings of 5-7pp are about 3-4 tasks: no CIs per release; count of regressed releases only in figure (tiers z=+/-0.75 sigma); numeric inconsistencies (peak 39.0% vs 39.4%; v0.5.0 32.5% vs 27%)

method: Same 35-release controlled design; normalised per-task efficiency
population: Qwen Code CLI, Qwen3-Next-80B-A3B-Instruct, 50 tasks x 2 runs
metric: Tokens per task; tool calls per task; LLM turns; trend
effect_size: Tokens: first nine releases about 391K per task vs latest about 668K (+70%); Spearman rho=0.743 p<0.0001 (normalised 0.751); trough 217K at v0.1.4; normalised range -24.2% to +19.6% of per-task mean; tool calls 6.9-14.3 per task; step-0 prompt payload +8%, LLM turns +18%, tokens-turns rho=0.941; unresolved tasks 697.7K tokens and 12.95 tool calls vs resolved 258.7K and 7.2. v0.1.4 to v0.1.5 +52% tokens (216.6K to 329.9K); v0.2.3 to v0.3.0 +131% (259K to 599.6K)
direction: Cost per task rose about 70% with no resolve-rate gain; failures cost about 2.7x tokens of successes
cost_data: Tokens and tool calls only; no currency or latency figures; Discussion text quotes different spikes (139% and 182%) from the RQ1 case studies (52% and 131%)
codebase_context: SWE-bench Verified, local model; prices not applicable
independence_flags: Academic
quality_notes: Internal inconsistency in spike percentages between Section 5.4 and Section 8.2; token counts are model-specific (a different model may tolerate prompt bloat differently)

method: Correlational attribution: 22 release-level factors and 10-component reference architecture vs quality shifts; Spearman, Mann-Whitney, Cliff's delta, BH-corrected; n=35 (delta n=34)
population: Qwen Code commits and PRs mapped to components by file path (churn split across components)
metric: Association of development patterns, components and PRs with resolve rate and efficiency
effect_size: Features: feat_churn_ratio rho=0.438 p=0.0075 with resolve rate but also tokens rho=0.401 and tool calls rho=0.360; refactor_churn_ratio rho=-0.372 p=0.025 with resolve rate; delta fix_churn_ratio vs tokens rho=0.339 Cliff d=-0.833; mean PR size vs tokens rho=-0.441 (delta); LLM Provider large change vs effectiveness rho=-0.336 (partial -0.221); Context Mgmt expansion vs token efficiency rho=-0.346 (partial -0.392); Security fixes vs efficiency rho about +0.34. PR cases: #969 and #981 (v0.1.5, +52% tokens), #1235 OpenAI converter change (v0.4.1 to v0.5.0, resolve rate 39.4% to 32.5%)
direction: Association not causation; moderate effects (absolute rho 0.33-0.55), many tests on 35 points; Provider and Context layers flagged as high-risk
codebase_context: One OSS TypeScript CLI; fast-moving project
independence_flags: Academic
quality_notes: Small n; component mapping by manual judgement; PR-level links are post-hoc narrative for a handful of releases, no ablation or revert test

method: Inspection of public CI/CD, test suites and GitHub Actions of Qwen Code (more than 300 unit/integration/e2e tests)
population: Qwen Code repo
metric: Whether regressions were catchable before release by project tests
effect_size: All documented regressions (+52% tokens v0.1.5, +131% v0.3.0, Provider-layer converter change with 39.4% to 32.5% resolve rate) passed all CI checks; no test evaluates resolve rate, token or tool-call budgets. Authors: 'could not have been detected by the project's public testing infrastructure'
direction: Functional CI does not detect agent-quality regressions; absence of agent-level regression testing is a plausible but not proven cause
cost_data: Authors attribute absence to cost of running agentic evals at commit cadence; no cost figures
independence_flags: Academic
quality_notes: Inspection of public CI only; private checks unknown; no test of whether an eval gate would have caught the regressions; cause stated as plausible not shown

method: Threats to validity as stated plus reviewer observations
population: Single harness, single open-weight model, 50-task subset
metric: Scope of inference

independence_flags: Academic; no funding statement found

method: Mixed-method qualitative: 13 think-aloud field observations (45 min + 30 min interview) plus 15-minute invited qualitative survey (n=99 of 249 responses from 4,141 emailed; 6% response); thematic analysis, no inter-rater reliability; data collected Aug-Oct 2025
population: 13 observed developers (>=3 yrs, median 9; 12 male; tools mainly Cursor 6, Claude Code 4, Copilot 2, Windsurf 1, Kilo Code 1, Codex 1; 5 production tasks, 3 exploratory R&D, 5 side/OSS) and 99 survey respondents (mean 12.8 yrs, median 10; 97 male; Asia 29, N America 27, Europe 24, S America 13, Africa 5, Oceania 1) recruited from AI-related GitHub repositories
task_types: T3; T4; T5; T6; T8 (task mix: 53 of 96 coded survey tasks were app building)
metric: Study design / sample characterisation
effect_size: n=13 observations; n=99 survey (104 qualified, 5 discarded as suspected AI-generated); 6% response rate; observation sessions 45 min

seniority_split: All participants >=3 yrs experience by selection; no junior comparison group

independence_flags: Academic, NSF-funded (grants 2432644, 2107397); no vendor funding; deliberate selection of AI-positive respondents; GitHub email scraping; sample nearly all male

method: Survey open coding of tasks named as suitable/unsuitable, 59 task codes appearing in >=5 surveys; suitability coded reflexively by authors with LLM-assisted quote retrieval; S:U = responses citing suitable vs unsuitable
population: 99 experienced developers (survey)
task_types: T3; T6; T10; T5; T8; T9 (delegated); T2; T4; T11 (kept or contested)
metric: Number of survey responses citing task as suitable (S) vs unsuitable (U)
effect_size: Suitable: writing tests 19:2; documentation 20:0; scaffolding/boilerplate 25:0; tedious/repetitive 26:0; refactoring general 18:3 and simple 14:0; simple debugging 12:3; prototyping 12:0; following well-defined plans 28:2; new project setup 10:4. Unsuitable: integrating with existing/legacy code 3:17; complex tasks 3:16; business logic/domain knowledge 2:15; replacing human decision making 0:12; CI/deployment 3:8; high-stakes or privacy-sensitive 0:8; security-critical 2:5; performance 3:9; complex refactoring/architecture 1:4; one-shotting without verification 5:23. Contested: high-level plans/architecture 13:23; general debugging 12:8; code review 7:4
direction: Agents suited to simple, repetitive, scaffolding tasks; suitability falls as complexity, implicit context and stakes rise; brownfield/legacy integration judged unsuitable more often than not
measurement_basis: self-reported (perceptions of suitability, not measured outcomes); one respondent may cite several tasks
seniority_split: Respondents all >=3 yrs; no split by seniority reported
codebase_context: Respondents' own contexts; legacy-code complaints (3:17) are mentions not rates; counts are mentions, not prevalence
independence_flags: Academic, NSF-funded; no vendor funding; recruited from AI-related GitHub repositories (AI-positive selection)
quality_notes: Academic; AI-enthusiast sampling frame likely inflates S counts; thresholds (2.5:1) chosen by authors' judgement; counts not mutually exclusive; authors note suitability may have shifted since study

method: Field observation coding (n=13) of prompts, plans and verification, plus survey open-ended responses (n=99)
population: 13 observed experienced developers; 99 survey respondents
task_types: T3; T4; T6; T8 (control practices span tasks)
metric: Control strategies used with agents
effect_size: All 13 of 13 observed controlled implementation at some level; 11 of 13 controlled design (the other 2 were debugging-only); 9 of 13 carefully reviewed every agentic change (all in own expertise domain); 3 of 13 (all on unfamiliar tasks) did not necessarily review code but monitored decisions and rejected dependencies; median 1.8 steps executed per prompt (max 5.0); 3 of 13 (P1, P2, P11) used plan files and context files; code diffs reviewed by 9 of 13 (P12 had no agent code); survey: 50 of 99 mentioned driving architecture/design, 43 clear context and explicit instructions, 18 user rules, 31 used multiple agents, mean self-reported frequency of modifying agent code 3.0 of 5
direction: Developers constrain agents with plan-first, small steps, diff review, tests and version control rather than autonomous operation
measurement_basis: observed (n=13: plans, steps, verification) and self-reported (survey counts, ratings)

seniority_split: Domain expertise cited as critical by 11 of 13 observed and 65 of 99 survey respondents; participants in familiar domains reviewed more closely
codebase_context: Mixed production, R&D and side projects; no codebase size/age data
independence_flags: Academic, NSF-funded; no vendor funding; recruited from AI-related GitHub repositories (AI-positive selection)
